atari:
Atari is one of the most legendary names in the history of video games — a brand that stood at the very birth of the gaming industry and became, for an entire generation, a synonym for the word „video game". For retro gamers, Atari is home to icons that defined how a game on a screen even looks and plays: from a simple bouncing ball through swarms of attacking centipedes to adrenaline-fueled races and tunnels of the future. It is a company that gave the world not only immortal arcade cabinets and the Atari 2600 home console, but also the handheld Lynx — and its logo with the jagged „Fuji" symbol still gives lovers of the classics goosebumps to this day.

## History

Atari was founded in 1972 in Sunnyvale, California, by **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**. The name comes from the Japanese board game go, where the term „atari" refers to a state similar to check in chess. The company kicked off the gaming revolution right away with its very first arcade cabinet, Pong (1972), whose simplicity and addictiveness launched an entire industry. In 1977 came a pivotal step — the Atari VCS home console, later renamed the Atari 2600. It brought video games into living rooms and became one of the most important consoles in history. Among its gems is the conversion of the arcade hit Centipede, in which the player fires at an endless centipede winding its way through a mushroom field — the pure essence of the golden age of arcade machines.

Atari also reigned over the arcade halls of the late 1970s and 1980s, where its division churned out one hit after another. After the famous crash of the gaming market in 1983, the company split up, and in 1984 it was bought by Jack Tramiel; thus Atari Corporation was born, while the arcade and development branch continued separately as Atari Games. It is from this era that many classics come, which later found excellent homes on the handheld Atari Lynx (1989) — the first color handheld with a backlit display. On the Lynx shone the wild combat race RoadBlasters, the dizzying pseudo-3D tunnel ride S.T.U.N. Runner, the brilliant „falling" puzzle game Klax with its unforgettable quips, the tactical artillery battle Rampart, and the action maze adventure Gauntlet: The Third Encounter.

## Key figures

At the roots of the company stands **Nolan Bushnell**, a visionary and co-founder whom many consider the father of the commercial gaming industry, and alongside him **Ted Dabney**. Pong was technically brought to life by engineer **Allan Alcorn**, whose simple yet brilliant design set off an entire era.

Among the most notable creators are **Dona Bailey** and **Ed Logg**, authors of the Centipede cabinet — Bailey was one of the few women programmers of her time, and the game became famous partly for its popularity among female players. Ed Logg is one of the most prolific designers at Atari Games; he signed his name to, among other things, the Gauntlet phenomenon and other arcade legends. In the field of puzzle games, **Dave Akers** together with **Mark Stephen Pierce** stood out as the creators of Klax. It is also worth mentioning **Jay Miles** and the team around the Lynx hardware, which grew out of the ideas of people previously connected with the Amiga company.

## Transformations and transfers

Few brands have gone through such a convoluted journey as Atari. After the company was split up in 1984, Atari Corporation (home computers and consoles like the Lynx and Jaguar) and Atari Games (arcade cabinets) existed in parallel, with the arcade branch after a time using the Tengen brand for the home market. Nolan Bushnell had meanwhile left the company back in the 1970s and later founded the Chuck E. Cheese chain and other ventures.

In 1996 Atari Corporation merged with the company JTS, which effectively meant the brand ceased to exist as an independent hardware player. Rights to the name traveled through Hasbro Interactive all the way to the French company Infogrames, which in 2003 renamed itself Atari in order to revive the famous brand. The arcade legacy (Atari Games) meanwhile passed through the hands of Time Warner and later transformed into Midway Games. Thus over the decades the famous logo changed owners like few other icons in gaming history.

## The present

Atari still exists in 2026, albeit in a form very distant from the original Californian company. Today's Atari SA, headquartered in France, primarily tends to the brand's rich legacy: it releases retro compilations, revives old classics, and focuses on nostalgia. In recent years the company has deliberately been buying up rights to old titles and brands — it has acquired, among others, the publisher Night Dive Studios specializing in the rescue and remastering of old games, the rights to a number of classic computer series, and the Intellivision brand itself. It has also released the retro console Atari VCS and the popular „plug-and-play" machine Atari 2600+, which can run original cartridges.

Atari has thus transformed from a technological pioneer into a curator of its own legend — a company that does not hide its past but builds upon it. For retro gamers this is good news: thanks to it, classics like Centipede, Klax, or S.T.U.N. Runner remain alive and available to new generations, instead of gathering dust in a museum of gaming history.
bitmap-brothers:
Among British game studios at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s, The Bitmap Brothers had no competition in one thing — style. This London crew built itself an image more like a rock band than a programming firm, had itself photographed in leather jackets and dark glasses, and its games looked so polished and sounded so energetic that on the Amiga, Atari ST, and in arcades you instantly recognize their signature. For retro gamers the studio is synonymous with futuristic sports, polished metal, aggressive techno, and merciless but fair gameplay. A brutal cosmic sport where goals are scored even with fists, a duo of barbarians hacking their way through layers of gods, and a team of mercenaries wading through a steampunk hell — all of this came out of one small British workshop that knew how to turn a retro game into an atmospheric experience.

## History

The Bitmap Brothers came into being in 1987, when **Mike Montgomery**, **Eric Matthews**, and **Steve Kelly** joined forces. The studio settled in London and from the start aimed at the then most powerful home computers — the Commodore Amiga and Atari ST, to which it later added versions for PC and other platforms.

The very first titles hinted that this was someone exceptional. *Xenon* (1988) was a brisk vertical shoot 'em up, and its sequel *Xenon 2: Megablast* (1989) then became famous not only for its smooth scrolling and detailed graphics, but also for music built on the licensed track „Megablast" by Bomb the Bass. The combination of polished action with the then-current dance sound became the studio's trademark.

The real triumph came in 1990 with the game *Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe*. This invented sport of the future — a combination of handball, rugby, and a street brawl — remains to this day one of the highest-rated games on the Amiga. Brutal duels, an elaborate team upgrade system, and the unforgettable roar of „Ice cream, ice cream!" from the stands made it an immortal classic. A year later, in 1991, came the superb platformer *Gods*, in which the player controls an ancient hero on a journey to immortality; it excelled with a clever „artificial intelligence" of difficulty that adapted to the player's skill.

The pinnacle of its work became *The Chaos Engine* from 1993 — a cooperative action game set in a dark steampunk Victorian world, where a pair of mercenaries clears a landscape infested by a frenzied machine. Excellent graphics, music by Richard Joseph, and the ability to play as a duo made it one of the most beloved titles of the entire Amiga era.

## Key figures

The face and soul of the studio were its founders. **Mike Montgomery** remained the main mainstay and technical brain of the firm for years, while **Eric Matthews** contributed to the design of key games including *Speedball 2* and *The Chaos Engine*. The third of the founding trio was **Steve Kelly**.

Of extraordinary importance for the sound of the games was composer **Richard Joseph**, whose music and sound effects — from atmospheric loops to the famous crowd shouts in *Speedball 2* — are inseparably part of the experience of their games. The early era of the studio was also strongly shaped by a graphic artist and programmer who stood at the birth of the characteristic visual style with metallic sheens and robust characters. It was precisely this care for detail, sound, and atmosphere that set the Bitmap Brothers apart from most of the competition of the time.

## The present

After its golden era on the Amiga, the studio tried to keep pace with the arrival of 3D, though with variable success. Among the later titles were, for example, the real-time strategy *Z* (1996) with its then-unusual degree of interactivity and humor, or *Speedball 2100* for the PlayStation. But the vision of the market was changing, and the small British studio had it ever harder against the budgets of the big publishers.

Eric Matthews gradually left the studio and devoted himself to other projects in the field. Mike Montgomery remained the most faithful to the brand — under the Bitmap Brothers banner, in later years he contributed to a new version of *Speedball 2* for modern platforms and continued to tend the studio's classic legacy.

In 2026 The Bitmap Brothers no longer count among active developers who would churn out big new games — their era belongs to the golden age of the Amiga. Nevertheless, their legacy has not disappeared. The classic titles have received official reissues and remasters on modern platforms, and names like *Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe*, *Gods*, and *The Chaos Engine* still appear in rankings of the best games of their time. For those who remember, the studio remains a symbol of an era when the British gaming scene set the tone for the whole world and when even a pixel game could be polished into the form of a true work of art. And every time „Ice cream, ice cream!" rings out from the speakers, a piece of that unmistakable bitmap era sounds along with it.
capcom:
Capcom is among the most legendary Japanese game publishers and developers of all. For retro gamers it is a name associated with the absolute top of the craft of the 8-bit and 16-bit eras: precise controls, uncompromising difficulty, and a visual style that ages only with grace. Whether it is the robot action of the Mega Man series, the brutal platformers Ghosts 'n Goblins, or the fighting-game genre that Capcom practically defined thanks to Street Fighter, this is a studio whose classics still belong among the very best you can play on an old console.

## History

The company came into being in Osaka in 1979 under the name I.R.M. Corporation and devoted itself to manufacturing electronic gaming machines. Under the name Capcom — an abbreviation of "Capsule Computers" — it began operating in 1983, when it threw itself fully into arcade cabinets. Soon came hits like 1942 (1984) and above all Ghosts 'n Goblins (1985), a gritty platformer with the knight Arthur that became a symbol of fair but merciless difficulty.

With the arrival of home consoles, Capcom quickly grasped the power of the new platform. On the NES it released the Mega Man series, whose second installment from 1988 is to this day considered by many to be the peak of the entire 8-bit era. Alongside its own brands, Capcom also shone with licensed titles based on Disney — DuckTales and Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers are among the most beloved games on the NES precisely thanks to Capcom's feel for platformer design. The 16-bit era brought further gems: to the SNES arrived Mega Man X, which recast the series into a faster and darker form, and the polished sequel to the hellish challenge, Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts. On the same console appeared also the atmospheric action game Demon's Crest and the Japanese RPG Breath of Fire II, while owners of the Sega Mega Drive could enjoy a great port of Ghouls 'n Ghosts.

The real revolution, however, was set off by the year 1991 and the arcade Street Fighter II. The game ignited a worldwide fever of versus fighting games, and Capcom became the absolute number one in this field. From it grew dozens of variations and spin-offs, among them the later Street Fighter Alpha. The studio capped off the 1990s on consoles like the Sega Saturn, PlayStation (to which arrived, for instance, Mega Man X4 and X5), and above all the Sega Dreamcast, on which Capcom developed its crossover fighting games.

## Key figures

Behind the birth of the firm stands entrepreneur **Kenzo Tsujimoto**, who founded Capcom and led it for decades. But the face of the classic era is above all **Tokuro Fujiwara**, a designer and producer who created the Ghosts 'n Goblins series and had a hand in many early hits. Among the legends belongs **Akira Kitamura**, lead designer of the first Mega Man, who defined the form of the blue robot.

An inseparable part of the brand became illustrator **Keiji Inafune**, the longtime face of the Mega Man series, who worked on it from the early installments and led it into the modern era. In the area of fighting games, producer and designer **Noshige Funamizu** stood out, along with the team around Street Fighter II led by **Akira Nishi**. The audio side was enriched by a number of composers gathered in the internal group Alph Lyla; the iconic soundtrack of Mega Man 2 was composed by **Takashi Tateishi**. These creators imprinted upon Capcom's games a characteristic signature that fans recognize at first sight and first listen.

## The present

Capcom still exists in 2026 and is doing better than almost ever — it is among the most successful and profitable Japanese publishers. It still resides in Osaka and remains an independent, publicly traded company; the firm is led by Haruhiro Tsujimoto, son of the founder. The studio today stands on strong pillars, among which stands out the phenomenal Monster Hunter series, whose roots reach precisely into the era that retro gamers remember, for instance, from the title Monster Hunter Freedom Unite on the PSP. Alongside it, brands like Resident Evil, Street Fighter (whose newest installment is among the pillars of the competitive scene), and Devil May Cry run at full throttle.

Importantly, Capcom actively tends to its rich history and has not tucked it away in a drawer. It regularly releases collector's collections and remasters of its classics — from the Mega Man Legacy Collection through Ghosts 'n Goblins anthologies to fighting-game compilations — so the legends described above are easily accessible to a new generation of players. For a lover of retro this is a rare combination: a studio that made history and yet to this day honors its own legacy.
epyx:
Epyx is one of those names that can bring a smile to the face of anyone who remembers the eight-bit era. For most players it is a studio inseparably tied to the Commodore 64 and to a series of sports games that turned the keyboard and joystick into instruments of a merciless battle for the best time. But Epyx wasn't only about sport — it was behind one of the toughest logic puzzles of its day, as well as a technologically pioneering handheld console. It is precisely this combination of ambition, playfulness and attention to detail that makes Epyx a legend which retro players still remember fondly today.

## History

The company was founded back in 1978 in California under its original name Automated Simulations. It was started by Jim Connelley and Jon Freeman, and initially focused on strategic and turn-based games, often with a fantasy flavor — famous, for example, was the Dunjonquest series with the title Temple of Apshai (1979), one of the first commercially successful computer RPGs.

The Epyx brand was at first used only as a distinguishing label for more action-oriented titles, but it gradually gained such weight that at the beginning of the 1980s the firm renamed itself completely. Under the new name and with a new direction, Epyx headed toward where it was meant to shine the most: arcade action and sport.

The golden era came in the mid-1980s. In 1984 Summer Games was released, which kicked off the hugely successful "Games" series. The peak of this lineage became California Games (1987) — a laid-back, sunny collection of disciplines such as surfing, skateboarding, BMX or frisbee throwing, which perfectly captured the atmosphere of the California lifestyle and became one of the best-selling titles for the Commodore 64 ever. From the same period is also Impossible Mission (1984), an action platformer with the digitized voice of the sinister Dr. Elvin Atombender and his line "Another visitor! Stay a while… stay forever!", which was forever etched into players' memories.

At the close of the 1980s Epyx threw itself into an ambitious hardware project. Under its wing a portable console with a color backlit display was created, which Atari eventually brought to market as the Atari Lynx (1989). Epyx supplied some of the key launch titles for it — the color edition of California Games was accompanied, for instance, by the brisk shooter Blue Lightning, the bizarrely entertaining Todd's Adventures in Slime World, or the brilliant logic game Chip's Challenge, today considered one of the flagship gems of the entire platform.

## Key figures

Among the founders were Jim Connelley and Jon Freeman; Freeman, together with Anne Westfall, stood behind the early strategy titles and later founded their own studio, Free Fall Associates. The face of Epyx's action era became the programmer and designer Dennis Caswell, author of the cult Impossible Mission, who gave the game its unmistakable atmosphere as well as its technically advanced solution for digitized speech. The logic gem Chip's Challenge was designed by Chuck Sommerville, who identifies with this game to this day and continues to work on it in later years. The composer and programmer Peter Engelbrite contributed to the musical and audio side of a number of titles, being, among other things, closely linked precisely with work for the Atari Lynx.

## Transformations and transfers

Epyx's path was far from straightforward. The costly development of the portable console, which Atari eventually took over, financially exhausted the firm, and at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s it ran into serious trouble. In 1989 Epyx declared bankruptcy and its star began to fade. In the following years the rights and the brand changed owners several times and passed between various proprietors and publishers, so the original studio essentially ceased to exist and survived only as a trade name on game boxes.

It is worth mentioning that Epyx's roots gave rise to other creative careers — the departure of Jon Freeman and Anne Westfall to Free Fall Associates is just one example of how talent from this incubator spilled out further across the entire gaming industry.

## Present day

Epyx as a living, functioning studio no longer exists today (2026) — its active era ended at the start of the 1990s. The brand, however, did not disappear entirely: the rights to it are in the hands of the Bridgestone Multimedia Group, which holds them more as part of a portfolio than as the basis of new game production.

Epyx's classic titles, however, live their real life elsewhere — in the community of retro players and collectors. California Games and Impossible Mission are among the most frequently recalled games of the eight-bit era, they appear in a wide variety of compilations and remasters, and they run on emulators as well as modern handheld consoles. Chip's Challenge, for its part, received an official re-release and a long-promised sequel from the original author. Epyx may thus have vanished from the business registers, but in the hearts of those who remember and on the screens of handhelds it lives on — exactly as a legend deserves.
game-freak:
There are few studios whose name has been inscribed into the history of gaming as indelibly as Game Freak. This Japanese company stands behind a phenomenon that outgrew the boundaries of video games and became one of the most valuable brands on the planet — behind Pokémon. For retro players, Game Freak is synonymous with hours spent at the handheld Game Boy, when friendships with the first one hundred and fifty creatures were born on the monochrome display and when the link cable connected two consoles and two friends. What began as the ambitious dream of a group of enthusiasts turned into one of the most enduring legacies of the eight- and sixteen-bit era.

## History

Game Freak originally arose as an amateur fan magazine about video games, written in the first half of the 1980s by Satoshi Tajiri and his friends. Tajiri, a passionate player of arcade games as well as a childhood insect collector, gradually moved from reviews to his own creations. Together with the illustrator Ken Sugimori he officially founded the company Game Freak in 1989. The studio first built a name for itself with smaller titles for Nintendo consoles, but Tajiri's heart project was a game inspired by his childhood hobby of catching bugs — an idea the team worked on with incredible patience for almost six years.

That project matured in 1996, when Pocket Monsters was released in Japan on the Game Boy. When the game reached the West two years later as Pokémon Red and Blue (and later Yellow with Pikachu inspired by the popular animated series), it triggered a worldwide fever. The brilliant move of two versions of the same game, which had to communicate with each other so the player could collect all the creatures, made the link cable an indispensable accessory.

The studio kept building on its success. In 1999 the second generation came in Japan, which the world got to know at the turn of the millennium as Pokémon Gold and Silver, later supplemented by the refined version Crystal for the color Game Boy Color. These installments added a day-and-night cycle, an internal clock and an entirely new region, and many players still consider them the peak of the classic era. With the arrival of the Game Boy Advance, Game Freak then opened the third generation with the games Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire (2002), to which the definitive edition Emerald was later added. And because the new hardware possibilities tempted a return to the roots, precise remakes of the original adventures were also created — Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen.

## Key figures

The soul of the whole studio has always been **Satoshi Tajiri**, a creative visionary whose childhood fascination with insect hunting gave rise to the entire idea of collecting and exchanging creatures. At his side stood and stands **Ken Sugimori**, the lead artist from whose hand the characteristic look of the first generations of creatures comes — it was his drawings that defined how Pokémon look.

The third essential figure is **Junichi Masuda**, who participated in the design of the games and above all composed their unforgettable music. The melodies from towns, caves and battles, which Masuda created still within the sound limitations of the Game Boy, were etched into players' memories just as much as the creatures themselves. Masuda gradually grew into one of the studio's leading creative forces and for many years was the face of the series toward the fans.

## Present day

Game Freak still exists in 2026 and remains the main developer of the mainline Pokémon games. The studio has retained its independence — it has not been swallowed up by Nintendo — and shares the brand within The Pokémon Company, which Game Freak co-owns alongside Nintendo and the company Creatures. This constellation has functioned essentially unchanged since the turn of the millennium and is among the most stable relationships in the whole industry.

Although Game Freak is inseparably tied to Pokémon, it has always allowed itself smaller projects outside the main series. A beautiful example from the Game Boy Advance era is **Drill Dozer** — a fresh action platformer about the girl Jill and her giant drill, which showed that the studio can captivate even outside the world of creatures. The studio continues in this tradition of experimental titles even today under the banner of the internal initiative Gear Project.

Even after more than three decades, Game Freak thus remains what it always was: a relatively intimate studio with an enormous heart, whose classic games for the Game Boy and Game Boy Advance still belong to the best that a retro player can experience on a handheld console.
hal-laboratory:
HAL Laboratory is one of those Japanese studios whose name may not be known to every player, but whose characters absolutely everyone knows. This unassuming development ace stands behind a pink ball named Kirby and took part in the birth of the Super Smash Bros. series — two pillars of Nintendo that make HAL one of the most important "second-party" studios in the firm's history. Retro players love HAL for their unmistakable feel for imaginative, accessible and yet surprisingly thoughtful design. Their games look adorable and play smoothly, but beneath the surface hides a mechanical precision that even seasoned veterans will appreciate.

## History

HAL Laboratory came into being in 1980 in Tokyo as a small group of enthusiasts fascinated by personal computers. The name reportedly refers to the fact that they wanted to be "one step ahead" of IBM — just like the computer HAL from the film 2001: A Space Odyssey (each letter one behind I, B, M). In the early years the firm devoted itself to software for home computers such as the Commodore VIC-20 and MSX.

The turning point came with the establishment of cooperation with Nintendo. HAL took part in creating games for the NES and gradually built a reputation as a reliable and creative partner. On the NES the logic games of the Adventures of Lolo series were released, in which the player, as the blue creature Lolo, solves cute but devilishly clever puzzles by pushing crates and collecting hearts — this trilogy still belongs today to the best that the puzzle genre offered on the eight-bit.

HAL truly became a legend, however, in 1992, when Kirby debuted on the Game Boy in the original Kirby's Dream Land. The pink hero capable of sucking in enemies caught on immediately, and just a year later received on the NES the grand sequel Kirby's Adventure, which was the first to introduce Kirby's iconic ability to copy the powers of swallowed enemies. This mechanic became the heart of the entire series. On the Game Boy it was then followed by Kirby's Dream Land 2, and on the SNES the acclaimed Kirby Super Star was released in 1996 — a compilation of several adventures with a splendid cooperative mode and a helper system, which many still consider the peak of the series' classic era.

## Key figures

The most prominent face of HAL is undoubtedly **Masahiro Sakurai**, who as a very young designer conceived Kirby and gave the series its characteristic playfulness and ingenious simplicity. Sakurai later also stood at the birth of the Super Smash Bros. series, which emerged from HAL Laboratory.

The second essential figure is **Satoru Iwata**. This brilliant programmer and later president of HAL managed to guide the studio through financial difficulties and contributed to the technical side of a number of projects. Iwata eventually became president of all of Nintendo — historically the first who did not come from the founding Yamauchi family — and is remembered to this day as one of the most beloved figures of the gaming industry. It was precisely Iwata's ability to combine programming brilliance with a human touch that became proverbial for both HAL and Nintendo.

Also worth mentioning are composers such as **Jun Ishikawa** and **Hirokazu Ando**, whose catchy melodies gave Kirby's adventures their unmistakable sonic signature.

## Transformations and transfers

At the turn of the 1980s and 1990s, HAL found itself in existential trouble and was threatened with collapse. Salvation came from a closer bond with Nintendo and an internal reorganization, in which Satoru Iwata himself took part, becoming president of the studio in 1993. When Iwata left in 2000 to go directly to Nintendo (and two years later became its president), HAL remained closely connected with the parent company.

An important moment was also the departure of Masahiro Sakurai, who left HAL Laboratory in 2003 to operate independently; nevertheless he continued to collaborate on the Kirby and Super Smash Bros. series as an external creator. Care for Kirby had meanwhile also given rise to the separate studio Flagship, and later above all HAL as the core guardian of the brand.

## Present day

HAL Laboratory still exists in 2026 and remains one of Nintendo's key internal partners. It is based in Tokyo and continues to care above all for the Kirby series, which with the arrival of newer consoles has also taken a confident step into the third dimension. In doing so, the studio preserves its traditional philosophy: to create games that are at first impression playful and accessible to anyone, but offer enough depth to entertain even the most demanding.

For retro players, HAL Laboratory remains a symbol of the era when adorable graphics and brilliant game design went hand in hand. Whether you fire up Kirby's Adventure on the NES today, or get tangled up in the puzzles of Adventures of Lolo, you will still feel that same honest craftsman's touch with which this studio won the hearts of players around the world.
intelligent-systems:
If there is a studio that can, with quiet confidence, craft a game that swallows dozens of hours of your life and stays with you forever, it is Japan's Intelligent Systems. This unassuming company, based in Kyoto, is one of Nintendo's closest allies and has for decades stood behind titles that pair thoughtful game systems with a surprisingly warm heart. Retro players love it precisely for that combination: behind seemingly simple graphics hides a depth that ages with grace. Whether it is turn-based strategy, a paper-craft adventure, or a puzzle diversion, Intelligent Systems has always honored the principle that gameplay is king.

## History

Intelligent Systems was founded in 1986 in Kyoto, just a stone's throw from Nintendo's headquarters, and from the outset was closely intertwined with it. In its early years the company helped with development tools and technologies for Nintendo, among other things contributing to the development of debugging hardware. Soon, however, it set out to create its own work and etched itself into gaming history as early as the late eighties.

The turning point was 1990, when *Fire Emblem: Ankoku Ryū to Hikari no Tsurugi* was released on the Famicom. This turn-based strategy with role-playing elements, in which fallen heroes stayed dead permanently, laid the foundations of an entire school of the genre. The *Fire Emblem* series long remained an exclusively Japanese affair, and only thanks to the characters Marth and Roy, who appeared in the fighting game *Super Smash Bros. Melee*, did interest in a Western release grow. The first installment to officially reach the West was thus the Game Boy Advance entry released under the plain title *Fire Emblem* (2003).

The nineties and the turn of the millennium rank among the studio's most prolific periods. In 1994 the cult shooter *Super Metroid*, on which Intelligent Systems collaborated, was created for the SNES. The studio also became famous for puzzle games from the Nintendo universe, among them the colorful matching puzzle *Pokémon Puzzle Challenge* for the Game Boy Color, which combined the catchy mechanic of falling blocks with the world of Pokémon.

On the Nintendo 64 came *Paper Mario* in 2000 (in Japan), a witty adventure with a paper-craft aesthetic that gave rise to one of Mario's most beloved spin-offs. And in 2001 another legendary series began in Japan: *Advance Wars*, a sharply tactical turn-based war on the Game Boy Advance that won legions of devoted fans in the West.

## Key Figures

Inseparably linked with Intelligent Systems is **Tōru Narihiro**, a longtime leading figure at the company, who was involved in a number of its projects and played an important role in the studio's relationship with Nintendo.

The face of the *Fire Emblem* series is **Shōzō Kaga**, the author of the original game, whose vision of a ruthlessly demanding strategy where a character's death truly means something defined the entire genre. After his departure, a new generation of creators took over leadership of the series; among them **Masahiro Higuchi** and Nintendo producer **Hitoshi Yamagami** stand out, who helped get the series on its feet during difficult years.

The composers deserve special mention. The music for the *Fire Emblem* series was long created by **Yuka Tsujiyoko**, whose orchestral and chamber motifs gave the games their unmistakably noble tone. The world of *Paper Mario* and other titles, in turn, was brought to life by sensitive, playful music that perfectly matched the visual style.

## The Present

Intelligent Systems still exists in 2026 and remains one of Nintendo's most trusted development partners. It is based in Kyoto and operates as a closely tied but independent studio, not as an internal Nintendo department; Nintendo, however, remains its main publisher.

The *Fire Emblem* series is today one of Nintendo's flagships. The installment *Fire Emblem: Awakening* (2012) saved the series from an uncertain future and turned it into a commercial phenomenon, followed by successful titles such as *Fire Emblem Fates*, *Three Houses*, and *Engage*. The studio continues to develop its other brands as well and tends to the *Paper Mario* brand together with other Nintendo partners.

For retro players, Intelligent Systems remains an example of a studio that never chased effect at any cost. Its games bet on clean gameplay, clever design, and a distinctive style, and that is exactly why we still gladly fire them up today, whether on the original hardware or on handhelds with emulation. It is a studio that proved that turn by turn, block by block, you can tell a story that endures.
konami-hideo-kojima:
When the name Konami comes up in retro circles alongside Hideo Kojima, it does not mean arcade machines or whips against vampires, but an entirely different school of game design – a school in which story and atmosphere matter just as much as the game itself. It was precisely within Konami that the young Kojima launched the Metal Gear series on the Japanese MSX computer and built the foundations of the stealth genre, that is, play based on sneaking around and avoiding enemies rather than head-on gunfire. For fans of the classics, this branch of Konami is a legend because it showed how deep and cinematic a video game experience could be as early as the eight-bit era – long before "storytelling in games" became a fashionable term.

## History

Hideo Kojima joined Konami in 1986 and almost immediately was put in charge of a project for the MSX2 computer platform. The result was Metal Gear (1987), a game that Kojima conceived against the conventions of the time: the player, in the role of soldier Solid Snake, was not meant to mow down enemies but to slip past them, hide, and advance unnoticed. This idea, born partly from the technical limits of the MSX, gave rise to the entire stealth genre. The game was a success and even got a conversion to the NES, though that was made without Kojima's direct supervision and diverged from the original in several respects.

On the MSX2, however, lies the sequel that many consider the true pinnacle of the eight-bit era: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake (1990). Here Kojima pushed everything further – he added stealthier mechanics, more sophisticated artificial intelligence for guards capable of hearing footsteps or spotting the player in an adjacent square, and above all a far more mature, almost espionage-thriller story. For years this game did not reach the West at all and became a semi-mythical grail for European and American players.

Kojima's work on the MSX, though, was not limited to military action. He also left a significant mark on the genre of adventures and visual novels. After the cyberpunk adventure Snatcher came SD Snatcher (1990), an RPG reworking of the same world with cutely rounded "super-deformed" characters, a combat system, and a surprisingly dark cyberpunk story about androids called snatchers. Here too Kojima's signature is visible: a strong emphasis on atmosphere, dialogue, and cinematic scene direction.

## Key Figures

The utterly central figure is of course Hideo Kojima – designer, writer, and director whose obsession with film seeps through every one of his titles. It was he who gave both Metal Gear and Snatcher their unmistakable tone.

The visual identity of the series was then fundamentally shaped by the artist Yoji Shinkawa, who joined Kojima later and became the go-to designer of characters and mechs. On the musical side, the Konami composing team deserves mention, whose sound capabilities on the MSX chip managed to coax suspenseful, cinematic melodies out of limited hardware, underscoring the stealthy play. Together these people formed the creative core from which a separate development group within Konami later grew.

## Transformations and Transfers

Kojima's creative cell gradually took shape as a distinct brand and within Konami eventually became the studio Kojima Productions, which for many years functioned as an internal development team. Under the Konami banner, Kojima led the Metal Gear series to worldwide fame on the PlayStation and other consoles.

The idyll was not to last forever, though. In 2015, after protracted disagreements, the paths of Konami and Hideo Kojima parted. Kojima left the company, spun off the Kojima Productions brand as an independent studio, and departed along with a number of key collaborators, among them Yoji Shinkawa. This closed one of the most distinctive chapters in the history of Japanese game development – an era when something as auteurist and singular as Metal Gear was created inside a large corporation.

## The Present

Konami still exists in 2026 as one of the great Japanese entertainment companies and holds the rights to the Metal Gear brand as well as to Kojima's other earlier titles created under its wing. In recent years the company has been rediscovering the value of its heritage and returning to classic series through collections and remakes. Hideo Kojima, meanwhile, continues on his own path at the independent Kojima Productions, outside Konami's structures.

For the retro community, however, that original Kojima era of Konami remains an untouchable classic. It was a period when Solid Snake was born on the modest MSX, when sneaking first took precedence over gunfire, and when games began to have the ambition to tell a story like a film. Metal Gear, its grand sequel, and the cyberpunk SD Snatcher still rank among the most precious things the eight-bit Japanese scene offered – and they remind us that some of the boldest ideas in the history of the medium arose within the tight constraints of long-forgotten hardware.

## Key Figures

The composing team Konami Kukeiha Club and figures such as Michiru Yamane, author of the unforgettable melodies of many Castlevanias, elevated game soundtracks to an artistic discipline. Distinctive humor and a singular style, in turn, were brought to games like Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon by the creators behind the zany series about the samurai hero Goemon.

## Transformations and Transfers

After 2010, Konami underwent a noticeable transformation. The company increasingly shifted the focus of its business toward pachinko machines, mobile games, and the fitness sector, which caused unease among part of its fan base. The peak of the tension was 2015, when, after protracted disputes, the paths of Konami and Hideo Kojima parted. ## The Present

Konami still exists in 2026 as one of the great Japanese entertainment companies and owns the rights to all its famous brands. Alongside video games, the company operates in arcade machines, sports, and a healthy lifestyle. For the retro community, however, Konami will forever remain the home of the Belmonts, the Contra brothers, and the sneaking Solid Snake – the creator of games that have passed the test of time and still rank among the best that eight-bit and sixteen-bit consoles offered.

Say the word Namco and every retro lover instantly pictures a handful of icons that changed the shape of the gaming industry forever. This Japanese company is behind the yellow glutton Pac-Man, behind the space shooter Galaga, and behind the fact that the arcades of the eighties breathed with color and catchy melodies. But Namco was not only a master of the arcades — when the era of home consoles arrived, it brought us brilliant racers, peerless fighting games, and dreamlike platformers. Retro players love it because wherever it stepped, it left behind a genre benchmark: whether you are sitting behind the wheel, swinging a sword, or leaping through cloudy worlds.

## History

Namco's story began unexpectedly — in 1955, when Masaya Nakamura founded Nakamura Manufacturing in Tokyo, a company that initially operated mechanical rocking horses on the roof of a department store. From a small operator of amusement attractions, it gradually became a maker of arcade machines. The turning point came at the end of the seventies: after the success of the shooter Galaxian (1979), Namco struck in 1980 with Pac-Man, one of the best-selling and most recognizable titles of all time. A year later came Galaga, revered to this day as the pinnacle of vertical shooters.

The eighties belonged to Namco in both technical and imaginative terms — Dig Dug, Pole Position, and Xevious pushed the boundaries of what an arcade machine could do. With the arrival of the nineties and 3D graphics, Namco did not fall behind; quite the opposite. Ridge Racer from 1993 showed what modern arcade racing should look like, and its later peak Ridge Racer Type 4 on the PlayStation charmed players not only with its driving but also with its unforgettable electronic soundtrack and stylish atmosphere. Just as pivotal was Tekken (1994), whose sequel Tekken 2 ranks among the jewels of the first PlayStation generation and defined 3D fighting games for decades to come. The peak of this craft became Soulcalibur, which in 1999 on the Dreamcast delivered weapon-based combat of a fluidity and beauty never seen before.

At the same time, Namco did not forget playfulness and imagination. The adorable hero Klonoa, with his long ears, first leapt into players' hearts in Klonoa: Door to Phantomile on the PlayStation, only to return later on the handheld Game Boy Advance in the adventure Klonoa: Empire of Dreams. These platformers proved that Namco could tell touching stories just as well as it could build perfect game mechanics.

## Key Figures

At the head of the whole story stands founder Masaya Nakamura, nicknamed "the father of Pac-Man" — a visionary who built a gaming empire out of rocking horses. Pac-Man himself was designed by the young designer Toru Iwatani, whose idea for a non-violent game that would also appeal to female audiences wrote itself into history. The characteristic sound and music of the early machines, including Pac-Man, was created by composer Toshio Kai.

Among the later creators, Shigeru Yokoyama stands out; he was present at the birth of the Tekken fighting series and gave it its face. In the field of racing games and music, a legend is the composer associated with the Ridge Racer series, whose dance and electronic tracks gave the brand its unmistakable sound. And no less important is Hideo Yoshizawa, the designer who brought the likeable Klonoa into the world and created his dreamlike world of Phantomile.

## Transformations and Transfers

Namco underwent one of the most significant transformations in the history of the Japanese gaming industry. In 2005 it merged with Bandai, a maker of toys and creator of brands such as Gundam, forming the holding group Namco Bandai (later renamed Bandai Namco). Game development was concentrated in the subsidiary Namco Bandai Games, which in 2015 adopted the unified name Bandai Namco Entertainment.

This merger meant the end of an independent Namco in the form that players of the eighties and nineties had known, but its legacy lives on under the new roof. Many key teams and creators remained and to this day develop the brands they once helped create. Masaya Nakamura himself remained an honorary figure associated with the company until his death in 2017.

## The Present

In 2026, Namco as a brand still lives on — only under the banner of the Bandai Namco Entertainment conglomerate, one of the largest Japanese publishers and developers. Under this name continue the series that made Namco famous: Tekken has seen modern installments with a worldwide tournament scene, Soulcalibur and Ridge Racer have their loyal fans, and Pac-Man appears in countless remasters, collections, and new variations.

Bandai Namco also cares for its retro heritage through collector's editions and official emulations of the classics, so both arcade legends and titles from the PlayStation and Dreamcast era can be revisited by new players too. For the retro community, Namco is proof that the courage to experiment — whether in an arcade in 1980 or on consoles two decades later — creates games that age with grace and remain fun even after decades.

Say "the best of what Nintendo can do" and almost invariably you are talking about the work of the Nintendo EAD team. This internal development division was present at the birth of nearly all the Japanese company's key brands and set the tone for the entire gaming industry for decades. From its workshop came the plumber Mario, the hero Link, and the whole legend of Zelda, and it was here that the games were born which to this day define what perfect game design means. Retro players love it because its titles have not aged: a platformer forty years old plays just as brilliantly as on release day, and its craftsmanlike precision remains the benchmark to which others look up.

## History

The team was formed in 1983 as part of a Nintendo reorganization under the name Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development. Its roots reach back to the legendary designer Shigeru Miyamoto, who had already become famous for the arcade hit Donkey Kong. It was in EAD that the title which changed history was born: **Super Mario Bros.** (1985) for the NES. Smooth jumping, brilliant level design, and unforgettable music made this work the best-selling game of its time and saved the gaming market after the crash of 1983.

EAD, however, was not a one-brand studio. As early as 1986 came **The Legend of Zelda**, with an open world and an emphasis on exploration that was revolutionary for its time. The end of the eighties was then crowned by **Super Mario Bros. 3** (1988), one of the best-tuned platforming experiences ever.

With the arrival of the Super Nintendo, the team moved even higher. The launch title **Super Mario World** (1990) introduced the dinosaur Yoshi, while **The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past** (1991) brought the action-adventure to perfection and became a model for the whole genre. EAD also broadened its portfolio further: the futuristic racer **F-Zero** showed what the Mode 7 graphics mode could do, and **Super Mario Kart** (1992) laid the foundation for one of the most successful racing series in history. Nor did the handheld consoles come up short, as evidenced by the charming **The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening** for the Game Boy.

The real breakthrough came with the arrival of 3D. **Super Mario 64** (1996) showed the whole industry what a hero's movement in three-dimensional space should look like, and to this day it is a textbook example of controls. Two years later came **The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time** (1998), which many critics still rank among the best games of all time. The Nintendo 64 era was closed by the darker and more inventive **Majora's Mask** (2000), the brisk **Mario Kart 64**, and the cosmic shooter **Star Fox 64**.

## Key Figures

The face of the studio was always **Shigeru Miyamoto**, father of Mario, Zelda, and Star Fox and perhaps the most influential game designer in history. His "play and have fun" approach permeated every project. At his side stood producer and director **Takashi Tezuka**, who contributed fundamentally to Mario and Zelda and gradually took over the lead on many key games.

The younger generation was represented by **Eiji Aonuma**, who became the central figure of the Zelda series starting with Ocarina of Time, and **Hideki Konno**, associated with the Mario Kart racing line. An unmistakable mark was also left by composer **Koji Kondo**, author of the iconic melodies from Super Mario and Zelda that even someone who has never played knows. These motifs rank among the most famous music in the history of the medium.

## Transformations and Transfers

Nintendo EAD was never an independent studio; it was always an internal division of Nintendo, so it avoided acquisitions or changes of ownership. It nevertheless evolved. Over time it grew into several development groups, and some of its people also worked in the satellite studio Nintendo EAD Tokyo, founded in 2003, from which came, for example, the new-generation 3D Mario games.

A fundamental formal change came in 2015. As part of a broader reorganization, Nintendo merged EAD with the Nintendo SPD division and created the new grouping **Nintendo EPD** (Entertainment Planning & Development). The EAD name thereby effectively ceased to exist, but the people themselves, the know-how, and the brands smoothly passed under the new banner.

## The Present

Today, in 2026, no games are released under the name Nintendo EAD anymore, but its legacy lives on within Nintendo EPD. This division is still Nintendo's largest and most important development team and stands behind modern hits from Mario through Zelda to Mario Kart. Shigeru Miyamoto remains in a leading role at Nintendo as a respected creative overseer, and Eiji Aonuma continues to lead the Zelda series. For retro players, however, what matters above all is that the classics the team once created are still alive, available, and just as entertaining as decades ago.

Say Nintendo R&D1 and the eyes of classic fans light up. This internal development division was Nintendo's oldest game studio and was present at the birth of some of the most influential brands in the history of the medium. It was here that Metroid was born, it was here that the Game Boy took shape, and it was here that the crazy universe of Wario later came into being. R&D1 was a place where technical ingenuity met the courage to go against the current, and retro players love it for repeatedly managing to redefine what could be experienced on a game console.

## History

The team's roots reach back to 1970, when the young engineer Gunpei Yokoi joined Nintendo and soon began leading the department that would grow into the Research & Development 1 division. Even before the era of video games, Yokoi made a name with toys and pocket electronics — above all the legendary Game & Watch line, which from 1980 taught the world to play anywhere and foreshadowed the whole philosophy of portable gaming.

In the eighties, R&D1 threw itself fully into video games. In 1986 came the title Metroid for the Famicom Disk System, a dark and lonely sci-fi expedition that introduced non-linear exploration of an interconnected world and became the foundation of the whole genre we now call metroidvania. Shortly before, in 1986, Kid Icarus was also released, a fantastical platformer about the little angel Pit that shared part of its technology with Metroid and earned its own cult status.

The true peak of Yokoi's career, however, became the Game Boy of 1989. Yokoi's principle of "lateral thinking with withered technology" — using cheap, proven, and economical components in a clever way — gave rise to a handheld console that, despite its black-and-white display, steamrolled its technically more advanced competition. R&D1 then stocked the handheld library with gems: the catchy Dr. Mario, the adventure Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins, and especially the title Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3 from 1994, which for the first time cast the greedy antihero Wario in the lead role. Samus also arrived on the handheld console in 1991 in the form of Metroid II: Return of Samus.

## Key Figures

The heart of the studio was without a doubt **Gunpei Yokoi** — inventor, designer, and mentor whose influence on the shape of Nintendo is hard to overstate. He raised a number of talents and imprinted on the team its characteristic combination of inventiveness and modesty of means.

Under his wing grew **Yoshio Sakamoto**, a director and writer who became the longtime face of the Metroid series and later of the WarioWare brand as well. It was Sakamoto who guided Samus through her further adventures and gave the stories of the bounty hunter their distinctive, often oppressive tone.

The graphics and gameplay side of the early games was contributed to by **Hiroji Kiyotake**, co-author of the design of Samus Aran and the character of Wario. The musical accompaniment to Metroid, which to this day ranks among the most atmospheric in gaming history, was composed by **Hirokazu Tanaka** — a composer whose electronic sound worlds gave the series its unmistakable identity.

## Transformations and Transfers

The fate of R&D1 is inseparably tied to the fate of its founder. After the commercial failure of the Virtual Boy console in 1995, Gunpei Yokoi left Nintendo in 1996 and founded his own company, Koto. He died tragically in a traffic accident in 1997, which was an enormous loss for the entire gaming industry.

The studio, however, carried on, and in the following years it was above all Sakamoto's team that upheld its legacy. At the turn of the millennium came further jewels: Wario Land 3 for the Game Boy Color (2000) and then, on the Game Boy Advance, the fresh trio of Wario Land 4 (2001), Metroid Fusion, and the remake Metroid: Zero Mission. In 2003, the crazy WarioWare, Inc.: Mega Microgame$! sprang from the R&D1 workshop, kicking off a whole sub-brand of micro-games.

In 2003, Nintendo underwent an internal reorganization of its development departments. R&D1 merged with other teams into the newly created division **Nintendo Software Planning & Development (SPD)**. With that, the independent "R&D1" brand formally ended, but the people and brands it had raised remained loyal to Nintendo.

## The Present

As a named division, Nintendo R&D1 no longer exists today — after the 2003 reorganization and the later merging of internal teams, its legacy dissolved into the structures Nintendo knows today (unified since 2015 under Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development, EPD). But the spirit of the studio lives on. Yoshio Sakamoto still works at Nintendo and oversaw the modern-day returns of Samus, including the acclaimed Metroid Dread of 2021. The brands that R&D1 built — Metroid, Wario, and WarioWare — remain pillars of Nintendo even in 2026. And so, even though the name on the door has vanished, every time you switch on an old Game Boy or Samus once again ventures into a planet's depths, a piece of the genius that this legendary division brought into the world of games resounds within it.

Nintendo is without a doubt the most legendary name in all of gaming history, and for retro players it represents something like the holy grail. The Japanese company is behind characters known even to people who have never held a controller in their lives: the plumber Mario, the hero Link, the voracious pink ball Kirby, and the sly Fox McCloud. Nintendo was never merely a maker of consoles; it was and is a workshop of ideas that has for decades defined what it actually means to "play." That is precisely why its name carries such weight among lovers of the classics, whether we are talking about hand-drawn handheld gems or grand adventures on big screens.

## History

Nintendo's story is far older than video games themselves. The company was founded in 1889 in Kyoto by Fusajiro Yamauchi as a maker of hanafuda playing cards. For decades it was a traditional card company, and only in the 1960s and 1970s, under the leadership of Hiroshi Yamauchi, did Nintendo begin experimenting with toys and electronic devices.

The turning point came at the turn of the 1970s and 1980s. In 1980 Nintendo introduced the Game & Watch line of handheld LCD games, whose simple but addictive titles such as Donkey Kong or the dual-screen Oil Panic became a cult phenomenon and at the same time a breeding ground for design ideas. It was Game & Watch that gave rise to the cross-shaped D-pad controller, which became the standard for the entire industry.

In 1981 Nintendo stormed the arcades with the hit Donkey Kong, in which a mustachioed hero later named Mario appeared for the first time. Two years later, in 1983, the Famicom console launched in Japan, which the world came to know from 1985 as the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The NES essentially put the modern gaming industry back on its feet, and classics were born on it such as Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda, and the snappy boxing arcade game brought home, Punch-Out!!.

An uninterrupted series of iconic machines followed. In 1989 the handheld Game Boy conquered the world, on which Tetris became a global phenomenon. The Super Nintendo (SNES) from the first half of the 1990s brought the golden era of 2D games, including the excellent Super Punch-Out!!. The Nintendo 64, GameCube, the dual-screen DS, and in 2006 the motion-controlled Wii then took turns pushing the boundaries of technology and gameplay. The Game Boy itself kept evolving: the color Game Boy Color hosted, for instance, a polished version of Tetris DX, and its successor, the Game Boy Advance, offered gems such as Super Mario Advance 4, which brought Super Mario Bros. 3 on the road.

## Key figures

The face of Nintendo for decades has been Shigeru Miyamoto, the brilliant designer behind the birth of Mario, Donkey Kong, Zelda, and Pikmin. His approach of "a game must above all be fun" permeates the entire company philosophy.

Alongside him, the legends include Gunpei Yokoi, inventor of the Game & Watch line and father of the Game Boy, whose philosophy of "mature technology used with lateral thinking" inspired generations of creators. Also worth mentioning is Hiroshi Yamauchi, the long-serving president who guided the company through its transformation into a gaming giant, and the charismatic Satoru Iwata, a programmer and later president who led Nintendo through the era of the DS and Wii until his untimely death in 2015.

The music is unforgettable too. Composer Koji Kondo wrote the main themes of Super Mario and Zelda, that is, tones that almost everyone recognizes today.

## The present

After more than a hundred and thirty years of existence, Nintendo remains at the top and stays an independent Japanese company headquartered in Kyoto. Its hybrid console, the Switch, introduced in 2017, became one of the best-selling gaming devices ever, and in 2024 the company announced its successor, the Switch 2, which arrived on the market in 2025.

Today's Nintendo has long been about more than just games. The brand expanded into film (the successful animated Super Mario movie from 2023), into theme parks in the form of the Super Nintendo World areas, and into mobile games. Yet the company retains its signature: attention to detail, family-friendly accessibility, and the ability to rediscover the joy of play again and again. What is more, it is a pleasure for retro players that Nintendo does not hide its rich past and offers classics from the NES, SNES, and Game Boy to new generations. The legend from Kyoto thus lives on, just as strong as in the days when Donkey Kong was chased across small LCD screens.

Among British game studios, Rare holds a privileged position — it is a company that managed to squeeze more out of Nintendo's consoles than anyone expected. For retro players, Rare is synonymous with technically astonishing, playful, and often slightly zany games that defined the SNES and Nintendo 64 era. Whether it was pre-rendered graphics that looked like they came from another planet on a sixteen-bit console, or sprawling 3D worlds full of collectibles and absurd humor, Rare had its own unmistakable signature. Their gorilla in a tie and the bear with a bird in his backpack remain among the most beloved characters of the classic era to this day.

## History

Rare's roots reach back to 1982, when brothers Tim and Chris Stamper, together with John Lathbury, founded the studio Ultimate Play the Game in Leicestershire, England. Under this label they released acclaimed games for the ZX Spectrum home computer, among them the cult *Jetpac* and *Knight Lore*. In 1985 the Stamper brothers founded a new company — Rare — and focused on the emerging console market, specifically on Nintendo.

Rare became one of the few Western studios that Nintendo fully trusted. In the era of the eight-bit NES they produced dozens of games, among which the relentlessly difficult action classic *Battletoads* from 1991 stands out. The real turning point, however, came in 1994 with *Donkey Kong Country* for the SNES. Thanks to the technique of pre-rendered 3D models converted into two-dimensional graphics, the game looked incredible by the standards of the time. It became a huge commercial hit and gave rise to an entire trilogy — *Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest* and *Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!* — which brought the series to perfection.

With the arrival of the Nintendo 64, Rare entered its golden era. *Blast Corps* (1997) entertained with its demolition of obstacles, the racing *Diddy Kong Racing* (1997) added a dragon and a battle mode to the go-karts, and in 1998 came the masterpiece *Banjo-Kazooie* — a colorful 3D platformer that remains among the peaks of the genre to this day. The studio did not forget more action-oriented tones either: the sci-fi shooter *Jet Force Gemini* (1999) showed that Rare could handle other registers too. It then carried its feel for detail to handheld consoles with titles such as *Donkey Kong Country* and *Conker's Pocket Tales* for the Game Boy Color.

## Key figures

The soul and the head of the studio were always brothers **Tim and Chris Stamper**, who set the creative and business direction from the Ultimate days all the way to the peak of the Nintendo 64 era. Tim Stamper was renowned for his design sense and the visual side of the games.

One cannot overlook composer **David Wise**, whose soundtracks for the *Donkey Kong Country* series — especially the atmospheric tracks from the second installment — rank among the most respected in the history of game music and still have devoted fans today. Among the studio's prominent figures was also **Gregg Mayles**, lead designer of *Banjo-Kazooie* and other key titles, who works at Rare to this day and has become one of its most enduring legends.

## Transformations and transfers

Rare's fate was fundamentally changed by the year 2002. Microsoft bought the studio for roughly 375 million dollars and moved it from the portfolio of Nintendo's collaborators under the wing of the Xbox brand. It was one of the most debated deals in the history of the industry — until then Nintendo had held a large stake in Rare, and fans feared what would become of the beloved studio. Some of the key figures soon left; some former employees later founded the studio Playtonic Games, which carried on the spirit of Rare's classic platformers with the game *Yooka-Laylee*.

The Stamper brothers stayed at Rare for some time after the acquisition, but definitively left it in 2007. That closed the era in which the studio was run by its founders.

## The present

Rare exists in 2026 as well and still belongs to Microsoft, today under the Xbox Game Studios division. In recent years it has been made famous above all by the online pirate game *Sea of Thieves*, which has built a large and loyal community. The studio also recalled its rich past with the retro collection *Rare Replay* (2015), which gathered dozens of classic titles from the Ultimate days onto a single disc.

After years of preparation, Rare also returned to its own iconic brand — with the fantasy action game *Everwild*, though its development was accompanied by a series of delays. For those who remember, Rare remains above all the studio that managed to coax miracles out of Nintendo's hardware and create characters and worlds that players loved for life. And even though today's Rare belongs to a different owner and makes different games, its golden era lives on in everyone who ever collected all the golden bananas or got lost in the music of underwater caves.

For retro players, Sega is something more than just a gaming brand — it is a symbol of an entire era and an eternal challenger that was not afraid to stand up to Nintendo face to face. The blue hedgehog, the slogan "Genesis does what Nintendon't," and the unmistakable voice shouting "SEGA!" when a game started etched themselves into the memory of millions of players around the world. For fans of the classics, Sega is the studio that gave arcades and home consoles speed, cheek, and a distinctive style: from the hellish action of Shinobi III through the dusty arenas of Golden Axe to the comic-book panels of Comix Zone. It is a company that made history both as a hardware manufacturer and as a brilliant game creator.

## History

Sega's roots reach surprisingly far — all the way back to 1960, when the company Service Games was established in Japan, from whose abbreviated name the name SEGA emerged. At first it devoted itself to making arcade machines, jukeboxes, and mechanical arcade devices. The real rise, however, came with the era of video games. In the 1980s Sega became one of the powerhouses of the arcade halls: titles such as Space Harrier (1985) showcased dazzling pseudo-3D graphics and became the flagship of an era in which designer Yuji Naka and producer Yu Suzuki pushed the boundaries of what arcades could do.

In the field of home consoles Sega first attacked with the eight-bit Master System. For it were created gems such as the platforming ride Alex Kidd in Miracle World, the magical adaptation Castle of Illusion with Mickey Mouse, and the original Phantasy Star (1987) — an RPG that was ahead of its time in its scope and its female protagonist. The true legend, however, was born with the arrival of the sixteen-bit console Mega Drive (Genesis in North America) at the end of the 1980s. It gave rise to the Sonic the Hedgehog series (1991), a mascot meant to rival Mario in speed and attitude — and it worked. The Mega Drive became home to immortal classics: the ninja action of Shinobi III, the brutal fantasy hack-and-slash Golden Axe, the inventive Comix Zone, where the player literally runs through the pages of a comic book, and the culmination of the famous RPG saga Phantasy Star IV. The handheld Game Gear could not go without the addictive puzzle game Columns.

The 1990s brought the 32-bit console Saturn with titles such as the nimble platformer Astal, whose hand-drawn graphics still captivate today. The Saturn, however, lost the battle with the PlayStation and foreshadowed harder times. The last console of its own was the visionary Dreamcast (1998), beloved to this day, which nonetheless drained Sega financially so much that in 2001 it withdrew from hardware production and became purely a developer and publisher of software.

## Key figures

The face of classic Sega is undoubtedly **Yuji Naka**, the programmer behind the Sonic the Hedgehog phenomenon, whom he created together with designer **Naoto Ohshima** (author of the look of the blue hedgehog) and level designer **Hirokazu Yasuhara**. This trio formed the core of the famous internal team Sonic Team.

No less important is **Yu Suzuki**, the brilliant creator of arcade hits such as Space Harrier, Hang-On, or Out Run, who later led the ambitious Shenmue project on the Dreamcast. Among the legends is also **Rieko Kodama**, a designer and director associated above all with the Phantasy Star series — one of the most distinctive female creators of the golden era of Japanese games. On the musical side, composer **Tomonori Sawada** and a number of other authors from the internal studio left their mark, whose melodies from Sega's arcades and consoles still ring in players' heads today.

## Transformations and transfers

Sega went through turbulent changes worth mentioning. After retreating from the hardware market, in 2004 it merged with the company Sammy and the holding Sega Sammy was created. At roughly the same time Yuji Naka left the company and later founded his own studio. Sega also absorbed a number of smaller teams and brands — under its wing belong, among others, the British Sports Interactive (Football Manager) and the studio Creative Assembly with the Total War series. Thus a Japanese console developer became a global publishing house with a diverse portfolio.

## The present

Sega is still alive in 2026 and doing well — it operates as part of the Sega Sammy group and remains one of the most prominent Japanese publishers. Sonic is once again at the peak of popularity, and not only thanks to games, but also to a successful film series that opened the door for the hedgehog to a new generation of fans. Alongside him, brands such as Like a Dragon (formerly Yakuza), Persona from the studio Atlus, which Sega owns, and the Total War strategies are running at full throttle.

For the lover of retro, however, the crucial thing is that Sega has not forgotten its rich legacy. It regularly releases collections and remasters of its classics — whether it is the extensive Sega Genesis Classics collections, or more ambitious projects reviving old brands. Thus players can today easily reach newer titles such as the strategic Valkyria Chronicles II from the PSP as well as old classics from the Mega Drive. Sega is living proof that even a company that lost the console war can remain a legend — and proudly lay claim to its past.
