square-enix:
When you say Japanese RPG, one single name pops into most gamers' heads – Square Enix. This company is behind series that defined the entire genre, from Final Fantasy through Dragon Quest to Kingdom Hearts. For retro fans, however, it is far more than just a publisher: it is the heir of two legendary studios whose rivalry and later union wrote a substantial part of the history of console games. Square Enix knows how to tell stories, compose unforgettable music, and build worlds to which players return even after decades. And that is exactly why we love it.

## History

The company in its present form was created in 2003 through the merger of two Japanese giants – Square and Enix. Each of them had a rich past behind it. Square (officially Square Co., Ltd.) was founded by Masafumi Miyamoto in 1986 and immediately wrote a piece of history: in 1987 it released the first installment of the Final Fantasy series. It is said the name was meant to symbolize the last attempt of a then financially exhausted studio – yet instead of an ending came enormous success and the birth of one of the most famous gaming brands ever.

Enix was a few years older, founded in 1975, and etched itself into players' memory above all thanks to the Dragon Quest series. Its first installment from 1986 practically invented the shape of the Japanese RPG as we know it today, and in Japan it became a cultural phenomenon comparable to a national holiday. While Square was renowned for technical and visual boldness, Enix bet on accessibility and warmth.

The nineties belonged to Square. Titles like Final Fantasy VI, Chrono Trigger, and Secret of Mana pushed the boundaries of what 16-bit hardware could do. The real turning point came in 1997 with Final Fantasy VII on the PlayStation – the game combined pre-rendered backgrounds, 3D characters, and a cinematic story, and opened the genre to Western audiences on a scale never seen before. After the two companies merged, the tradition continued: on the PSP, for example, the prequel Crisis Core: Final Fantasy VII was released, offering players the story of the soldier Zack Fair and rounding out the legend surrounding the seventh installment.

## Key figures

The face of Final Fantasy has always been Hironobu Sakaguchi, the father of the whole series and the spiritual leader of the classic Square. Beside him one cannot overlook artist Yoshitaka Amano, whose ethereal illustrations gave the brand an unmistakable visual style, nor character designer Tetsuya Nomura, who is behind the modern look of the heroes and stands behind the Kingdom Hearts series.

Completely essential is composer Nobuo Uematsu. His music for dozens of Final Fantasy installments ranks among the best that has ever sounded in the gaming medium, and a melody like "Aerith's Theme" is known even by many people who have never played the game. On the Enix side, one cannot pass over composer Koichi Sugiyama and mangaka Akira Toriyama, author of Dragon Ball, whose characteristic drawing style still adorns the entire Dragon Quest series.

A special mention deserves Yasumi Matsuno, a designer famed for elaborate, tactically demanding games with mature storytelling. He is behind Final Fantasy Tactics as well as the reworked version of Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together, a pair of titles that found perhaps their best home on the PSP – in the case of the tactical Final Fantasy in the form of the polished edition The War of the Lions with a new translation and animated scenes.

## Transformations and transfers

The union of Square and Enix in 2003 was in itself an enormous event – two longtime rivals became one company. The group continued to grow: in 2005 it bought Taito, the famous creator of arcade classics and Space Invaders, and in 2009 it acquired the British-Japanese Eidos, thereby bringing under its wing Western brands like Tomb Raider, Hitman, and Deus Ex.

The changes did not spare the founders either. Hironobu Sakaguchi left the company after the failure of the film Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within and in 2004 founded his own studio, Mistwalker. Nobuo Uematsu also went independent and devoted himself to his own projects, though he continued to contribute occasionally to commissions for Square Enix. These departures symbolically closed one era and opened another.

## The present

Square Enix still exists in 2026 and remains one of the most important players in the field of RPGs. Both Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest continue in new installments, remasters, and remakes – the grand reworkings of Final Fantasy VII proved that the company can resurrect a classic for a new generation without losing the soul of the original. A remarkable step was the sale of its Western studios and brands (Eidos, Crystal Dynamics, and related titles) to the Embracer group in 2022, with which Square Enix partly returned to its Japanese roots and focuses on what it does best. For retro gamers it remains a sure thing: whether you reach for an old classic or for its modern reincarnation, the name Square Enix still means a story, music, and a world that grows dear to your heart.
square:
If there is a single name that, for an entire generation of gamers, embodies the Japanese RPG, it is Square. The studio, which entered history above all thanks to the Final Fantasy series, managed to create, on eight-bit and sixteen-bit consoles, worlds with such depth of story, music, and emotion that players carry them in their hearts to this day. Square was not just a maker of games — it was a house in which gaming began to be taken seriously as storytelling. For retro enthusiasts it represents the golden era when simple entertainment became art and when a cartridge in a console could bring tears to your eyes.

## History

Square (in Japanese Square Co., Ltd., built on the Squaresoft brand) was founded in 1986, when it became independent from the original software division of the firm Den-Yu-Sha, owned by Masafumi Miyamoto. It was Miyamoto who founded the company and stood at its uncertain beginnings. At the end of the 1980s the studio was in financial trouble, and according to a now legendary tale, one of its young employees, Hironobu Sakaguchi, decided to bet everything on a single card. He aptly named the game he was preparing Final Fantasy — it was to be his last game if the studio failed.

The opposite came true. Final Fantasy was released on the Nintendo Entertainment System in 1987 (in North America then in 1990) and became a blockbuster that saved the studio and set it on a path that continues to this day. In the Super Nintendo era, Square literally flourished. A number of Final Fantasy installments were released here — IV (in North America released as Final Fantasy II) in 1991, V two years later, and in 1994 the monumental Final Fantasy VI, which many still consider the peak of the classic, two-dimensional JRPG.

But Square never confined itself to a single series. In parallel it developed the Seiken Densetsu brand, known in the West under names like Mystic Quest, Secret of Mana, and Trials of Mana. The first installment, Final Fantasy Adventure for the Game Boy, opened a more action-oriented, real-time take on the RPG, followed by the gorgeous Secret of Mana on the SNES with the option of multiplayer cooperation. The culmination of this line was Seiken Densetsu 3 — an installment that Japanese players already loved in the 1990s, while the rest of the world officially got it only much later under the name Trials of Mana.

## Key figures

The face of Square is undoubtedly Hironobu Sakaguchi, the father of the Final Fantasy series, who for many years oversaw its direction as producer and director. At his side stood other creators whose names still resonate today. Akitoshi Kawazu contributed to the game systems of the early installments and later developed his own SaGa series. Hiroyuki Ito was behind elaborate combat systems, among others the famous Active Time Battle.

The visual soul of the studio was Yoshitaka Amano, whose ethereal, dreamlike illustrations gave Final Fantasy an instantly recognizable face. An absolutely essential figure, however, is composer Nobuo Uematsu — his music for Final Fantasy VI and other installments ranks among the best ever created in game music, and for many players it is inseparable from the experience itself. To the younger generation belongs Yasumi Matsuno, author of strategically rich titles, whose signature is borne even by tactical installments like the later Final Fantasy Tactics Advance on the Game Boy Advance.

## Transformations and transfers

The fate of Square is closely tied to its longtime rival — the studio Enix, publisher of the competing Dragon Quest series. After the costly and commercially unsuccessful film Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within (2001), Square found itself in financial distress, and the two companies, long seen as archrivals, merged in April 2003 into the new company Square Enix.

This merger meant the end of the Squaresoft brand as an independent entity, but at the same time the birth of one of the most powerful players in the field of RPGs. Founder Hironobu Sakaguchi did not remain at the studio permanently after the merger — he left and later founded his own studio, Mistwalker, under which he created games like Blue Dragon and Lost Odyssey. Composer Nobuo Uematsu also gradually became independent and began working as a freelance author, though he continued to collaborate on music for Square Enix.

## The present

Square's legacy is today carried by the company Square Enix, which in 2026 still ranks among the most important Japanese game studios and publishers. The Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest series continue on, remakes and entirely new installments are being made, and classic titles appear on modern platforms through collections and digital stores.

The standalone Square brand did formally cease to exist in 2003, but its legacy lives on in every new JRPG that tries to combine a grand story with unforgettable music. For retro gamers, Square remains synonymous with the era when the Japanese RPG reached its artistic peak — and cartridges like Final Fantasy VI or Secret of Mana are still the best proof of it.

There are studios that flooded the market with dozens of titles, and then there are companies like Sunsoft — a Japanese brand whose catalog may not be endless, but whose best games rank among the most finely crafted the 8-bit and 16-bit eras had to offer. Retro players didn't fall in love with Sunsoft for its quantity, but for a peculiar craftsmanly integrity: this brand knew how to squeeze graphics, animation and, above all, music out of the limited NES or Game Boy hardware that the competition took a long time to catch up with. When the name Sunsoft comes up today, fans think of the bombastic bass sound of the Famicom chip, playful animations, and a handful of games that have over time attained near-cult status.

## History

The company's roots reach further back than one might expect. The parent company **Sun Electronics** (Sun Denshi in Japanese) was founded as early as April 1971 in Aichi Prefecture as a manufacturer and seller of electronics. It entered the gaming business in October 1978, when its first arcade machines arrived in the arcades. The real breakthrough, however, came only in the mid-1980s, when the company threw itself into home consoles — above all the Nintendo Famicom. It was then, around 1985 and the title *Super Arabian*, that the **Sunsoft** brand was born, under which games for players at home and abroad have been released ever since.

The second half of the 1980s and the start of the 1990s were a golden period for Sunsoft. In 1988, *Blaster Master* was released on the NES — a genre hybrid that combined driving a battle vehicle with on-foot action segments viewed from above and from the side, and became one of the studio's most acclaimed games ever. Sunsoft also built a reputation as a reliable license holder: it ported a number of Sega titles like *Fantasy Zone* and *After Burner* to Nintendo consoles and later acquired prestigious licenses such as *Batman* and *The Addams Family*.

The pinnacle of craftsmanly virtuosity is the now-legendary *Gimmick!* from 1992 — a late NES title with the adorable sprite Yumetaro, the ingenious physics of the star the player launches, and a soundtrack that used an add-on sound chip and remains one of the most frequently cited examples of what the Famicom could do. Two years later, in 1994, the tender platformer *Trip World* came out on the Game Boy, where the hero Yacopu transforms into various forms; for its beauty, calm and rarity it became a sought-after collector's gem.

## Key figures

Sunsoft became renowned as a studio where composers stood out. The name **Naoki Kodaka** is inextricably linked with the era of NES titles — he is behind the music of games like *Blaster Master*, *Batman* and *Journey to Silius*, and his bass lines became a hallmark of the brand. Alongside him, composers such as **Nobuyuki Hara** and **Shinichi Seya** also contributed to the sound, helping to develop the characteristic "Sunsoft" sound that made full use of the sound hardware's capabilities.

In the more recent era, the face of the brand became **Yuichi Ochi**, general manager of Sunsoft, who in 2021 announced the company's return to the gaming scene and became the voice of the entire reborn brand.

## Transformations and transfers

Sunsoft was never an independent company in the true sense of the word — it always operated as the gaming division of the Japanese Sun Corporation (Sun Denshi). A fundamental turning point came in 1995, when the American branch **Sun Corporation of America** found itself on the brink of bankruptcy and was dissolved; overseas operations thereby practically ended. The Japanese headquarters, however, survived, and in the following years it reoriented itself toward pachinko, mahjong, RPGs and mobile games, often in cooperation with partners like NTT DoCoMo. Sunsoft thus withdrew from the limelight of big console hits into the background for many years, without ever completely disappearing.

## The present

To the delight of fans, Sunsoft has revived in recent years. In August 2021 the company announced its rebirth under the slogan "Sunsoft is Back," and since then it has consistently cared for its classic legacy. Earlier, in 2017, the successful *Blaster Master Zero* series launched in cooperation with the studio Inti Creates, which revived the NES legend in a modern way and saw three installments. Other projects followed — for example *Ikki Unite* from 2023, a playful reworking of an old Famicom game into a form close to the modern "survivors" genre.

Sunsoft also returned to its treasures: in cooperation with Limited Run Games, a remaster of *Trip World* was released with a full-color version for the Game Boy Color, on which the game's original creator collaborated. In 2024 the collection *Sunsoft is Back! Retro Game Selection* arrived, which for the first time made several early Famicom titles available outside Japan with an English translation. As of 2026, then, Sunsoft continues to exist as part of Japan's Sun Corporation, and after years of silence it once again ranks among the brands the retro community follows with genuine hope — because a studio that once created *Gimmick!* and *Blaster Master* certainly deserves the attention.
taito:
When you say Taito, retro players smile and the unmistakable "whoever destroys the block first" instantly rings out in their heads. This Japanese company is one of the oldest in the entire gaming industry, and its imprint on the history of arcades is indelible. Taito is behind Space Invaders — the game that literally kicked off the golden era of video games and emptied the pockets of an entire generation. But it is also behind the endlessly catchy Bubble Bobble and the brick-breaking of Arkanoid, that is, titles that to this day rank among the best that arcades and home computers had to offer. Retro enthusiasts love Taito precisely for that combination: a simple rule, devilish addictiveness, and melodies that burrow under your skin for life.

## History

Taito's roots reach surprisingly deep — the company was founded in Tokyo in 1953 by the Russian entrepreneur Michael Kogan under the name Taito Trading Company. At first it dealt in importing goods and manufacturing vending machines, gradually moving on to amusement machines. The pivotal moment came in 1978, when designer Tomohiro Nishikado created Space Invaders. The game became a worldwide phenomenon, reportedly caused a coin shortage in Japan, and forever showed the potential dormant in video games.

But Taito was not a one-hit company. In the 1980s it churned out one arcade classic after another. In 1986 came Arkanoid, an ingenious modernization of the old Breakout with a paddle called the Vaus, vanishing bricks, and a series of gimmicks that changed the pace of the game. It soon moved from the arcades to all the home platforms of the time — from 8-bit Ataris to the Commodore 64 — and years later, in the form of Arkanoid: Doh It Again, it returned to the Game Boy so players could enjoy it on the go. Later that same year, 1986, Bubble Bobble saw the light of day, a magical cooperative platformer with the little dragons Bub and Bob, who trap enemies in bubbles. It became a symbol of shared fun at a single arcade machine and remains to this day the benchmark for how a two-player game should look.

The 1990s brought further gems — the Bubble Bobble sequel titled Rainbow Islands, the hectic Puzzle Bobble (known elsewhere as Bust-A-Move), in which you shoot colored bubbles, and the brisk horizontal shooters of the Darius series with their characteristic mechanical fish. Taito also operated the renowned Taito Station game centers, thanks to which the brand remained tied to Japanese gaming culture even beyond the games themselves.

## Key figures

At the head of the whole story stands founder Michael Kogan, who gave the company its name and international outlook. The face of the gaming legacy, however, is Tomohiro Nishikado — the engineer and designer who not only designed Space Invaders but practically programmed the whole thing himself, including his own hardware. He belongs among the true pioneers of the field.

An unmissable presence is the composing group Zuntata, Taito's in-house musical body founded in the mid-1980s. It is Zuntata that stands behind the unmistakable soundtracks of the Darius series and many other titles, and it holds a cult status among fans of retro music. Music thus became one of the brand's hallmarks — Taito never treated sound as a by-product, but as a full-fledged part of the experience.

## Transformations and transfers

Taito underwent a fundamental change of owner. After decades of independent existence, it was bought in 2005 by the Japanese company Square Enix, best known for the Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest series. Taito became its subsidiary and gradually focused primarily on operating arcade parlors and on mobile and online games.

This acquisition meant the end of Taito as the independent giant it had been in the golden era of arcade machines, but the brand as such did not disappear — on the contrary, it gained the strong backing of a large publisher. Its rich catalog of classics thereby passed under the wings of Square Enix, which continues to look after it.

## The present

In 2026 Taito still exists, as a subsidiary of the Square Enix group. It focuses mainly on the Japanese market — it operates the extensive network of Taito Station arcades, develops and publishes mobile games, and looks after its valuable archive. The classic titles have not been forgotten: Taito makes them available to modern players through collectible compilations such as the Egret II Mini (a miniature replica of a period arcade cabinet) or the range of digital releases of Space Invaders and other legends for current consoles.

For the retro community, Taito remains one of the most important names of all. Without Space Invaders the gaming industry would look different, and without Bubble Bobble or Arkanoid, collections of classics would be poorer. It is a studio whose games can be described in a single sentence but played for whole hours — and it is precisely in that timeless simplicity that the magic lies, the reason players keep coming back to them even after decades.
treasure:
There is a handful of game studios whose name works as a guarantee of quality, and Treasure belongs among them without the slightest reservation. These Japanese creators earned a reputation as masters of action who never took the path of least resistance: instead of safe sequels they churned out bold, original and technically superb games in which every boss fight feels like a meticulously rehearsed piece of theatre. For lovers of run-and-gun shooters, hectic shoot 'em ups and wildly inventive design, Treasure is a little idol. The studio managed to turn a handful of people into titles that are still studied today as textbook examples of what a craftsman-perfect 2D action game should look like.

## History

Treasure was founded in 1992, and its birth is a legend in itself. A group of developers left Konami because they were tired of the endless milking of established franchises and longed to create their own, new games. Their very first effort left no one in doubt that something exceptional had arrived: Gunstar Heroes (1993) on the Sega Mega Drive is still regarded as one of the best action games of its generation. The brisk run-and-gun shooter dazzled with smooth animation, inventive weapon combinations and boss fights that pushed the sixteen-bit hardware to the very edge of its capabilities.

Treasure quickly became synonymous with games that squeezed the maximum out of consoles. The Mega Drive saw a surreal platforming gem, Dynamite Headdy (1994), with a hero who swaps heads like hats, and above all Alien Soldier (1995) — a relentless parade of boss fights that even today ranks among the most demanding and spectacular titles ever released on a Sega system. This is where the studio's signature came fully into view: minimal "filler" between the action highlights and an emphasis on unforgettable, choreographically thought-out battles.

With the arrival of a new generation the studio elegantly moved into the 32-bit era. The Sega Saturn saw Guardian Heroes in 1996, a combination of beat 'em up and RPG with a branching story and co-op play that players still love today. That same year brought Radiant Silvergun, a vertical shoot 'em up considered one of the pinnacles of the entire genre — its complex shooting system and elaborate story made it a sought-after gem among collectors. Treasure continued this line on the Dreamcast with Ikaruga (2001), a brilliantly simple yet devilishly hard "danmaku" built around switching between black and white polarity. Ikaruga became probably the studio's most famous game and to this day is regarded as the holy grail of the genre. The Dreamcast also received the boisterous, explosive Bangai-O (1999), further proof that Treasure knows how to turn on-screen chaos into refined fun.

The studio did not forget handheld consoles either. For the Game Boy Advance it created Gunstar Super Heroes in 2005, a tribute and spiritual successor to the famous first installment that carried all the energy of the original onto the small screen.

## Key figures

Behind the founding of Treasure stands Masato Maegawa, the studio's longtime president, who once summoned the courage to leave Konami and bet on creative freedom. It was his leadership that kept the studio small, cohesive and true to its own vision even in times when the competition was growing to gigantic proportions.

The face of the studio's game design is Hiroshi Iuchi, author and director of the iconic shooters Radiant Silvergun and Ikaruga, who also contributed to their visual and musical sides. Among other key creators is Tetsuhiko Kikuchi (known by the nickname Han), an artist and designer with a hand in a number of classics including Gunstar Heroes. This well-coordinated band of veterans, many of whom had already been through Konami together, gave the studio its unmistakable character: an obsession with detail, a sense for spectacular battles and a taste for trying what others did not dare.

## The present

Treasure still exists in 2026, albeit much more quietly than in the 1990s. The studio remains independent and small, faithful to its philosophy of quality over quantity, and it never let itself be swallowed by a larger publisher. It releases new games only rarely, but it manages its heritage all the more carefully. Classics such as Ikaruga have received new releases on modern platforms, where they are discovered by further generations of players, and Gunstar Heroes regularly comes back to life in retro collections and digital re-releases. For the retro community, Treasure is enduring proof that the size of a studio does not matter — what matters is heart, craft and the courage to create differently. Few brands have managed to keep such unconditional respect from fans as those who once left to build their own treasures.
westwood-studios:
If there is a studio whose imprint is felt by anyone who ever built a base, harvested resources and sent tanks against the enemy, it is **Westwood Studios**. These enthusiasts from desert Las Vegas essentially invented modern real-time strategy in the form we know today, and before that they dragged us into the darkest dungeons that eight-bit and sixteen-bit computers were able to render. For retro gamers, Westwood is synonymous with the golden era of PC games: a combination of technical daring, music that burrowed into memory, and game design that was ahead of its time. It is no accident that their classics still run today on emulators as well as in modern remasters.

## History

The studio was founded in **1985** under the name **Westwood Associates** in Las Vegas, and at its birth stood two men who would shape entire genres: **Brett Sperry** and **Louis Castle**. They started modestly, porting and developing games for other publishers, but they soon built a reputation as a reliable and inventive team.

They left their first big mark in the dungeon crawler genre. **Eye of the Beholder** (Amiga, 1991) brought the rules of Advanced Dungeons & Dragons into a smooth first-person view and instantly became a benchmark of the genre. That same year came the sequel **Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon** (Amiga, 1991), which many still consider the peak of the series, whether for its atmosphere or for its more ingenious puzzles and battles.

The real turning point, however, came in **1992** with the game **Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty** (Amiga, 1992). It loosely followed the world of Frank Herbert, but it entered history for something else: it defined the template of modern real-time strategy. Harvesting resources (the precious spice), building a base, producing units and controlling with a mouse in real time — everything we take for granted today was here assembled together by Westwood for the first time in a coherent way.

On this foundation the studio then built its most famous legacy. In **1995** came **Command & Conquer**, which transformed the principles from Dune II into a full-fledged strategy series with cult live-action video sequences and two rival factions. A year later followed **Command & Conquer: Red Alert** (1996), an alternate history of the Cold War that won an enormous fan base. At the same time Westwood did not forget its RPG roots and developed the **Lands of Lore** series, beginning with **Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos** (1993).

## Key figures

At the head of the studio throughout stood its founders. **Brett Sperry** was the driving engine of vision and game design — he is even credited with the very name Command & Conquer. **Louis Castle** established himself as the technological and creative leader who helped the studio push the boundaries of what the computers of the day could handle.

No memory of Westwood, however, is complete without **Frank Klepacki**. This composer and musician gave the Command & Conquer and Red Alert series their unmistakable sound — an energetic mix of rock, industrial and electronica. His track **"Hell March"** from Red Alert ranks among the most iconic game music ever and to this day gives goosebumps to everyone who ever commanded both Soviet and Allied armies.

## Transformations and transfers

Like many successful studios, Westwood too passed through several owners. First it came under the wing of the publisher **Virgin Interactive**, which was behind the release of its flagship titles in the 1990s. The real turning point in the ownership structure came in **1998**, when the studio was bought by the gaming giant **Electronic Arts**.

The merger with EA brought the backing of a large publisher, but also gradual tension. In **2003** Electronic Arts **closed** the Westwood studio and absorbed part of its creative legacy into its own teams. For many fans it was the sad end of an era. The development talent, however, did not vanish — new studios emerged from the ranks of former employees, among them **Petroglyph Games** and **Jet Set Games**, which went on to develop strategic and other gaming traditions in their own projects.

## The present

Westwood Studios as a company has not existed since **2003**, but its legacy lives on, and surprisingly strongly. The real-time strategy genre, which the studio practically co-created, has influenced hundreds of games, and entire successor studios stand on people who once passed through the desert offices in Las Vegas (as of 2026).

For the retro community an important moment was the year **2020**, when the **Command & Conquer Remastered Collection** was released — a carefully renovated edition of the original Command & Conquer and Red Alert, which Louis Castle also helped work on and which delighted veterans and a new generation of players alike. It is a beautiful proof that good design does not age: whether today you launch Eye of the Beholder on an emulated Amiga or build refineries in Dune II, you are reaching for games that wrote history. And that is precisely why Westwood Studios has never quite closed its gates in the hearts of retro gamers.
atlus:
Atlus is a Japanese development studio that, starting out as a smaller and long rather niche publisher, built itself a reputation as one of the most distinctive creators of Japanese RPGs. While the big players in the market bet on mass-market fantasy series, Atlus took the path of darker, more philosophical and stylistically bold worlds tied to occultism, demons and existential themes — led by the long-running Shin Megami Tensei series and its most successful branch, Persona. Persona, which blends a school-life simulator with tactical combat, has in recent years become one of the most distinctive hits in Japanese game design and has brought Atlus to the attention of a far wider audience than the studio had for most of its history.

## History

Atlus was founded in Japan and in its early years established itself as a smaller developer focused on handheld and home console games, gradually building up its flagship Shin Megami Tensei series, built on collecting and negotiating with demons and a darker, more mature atmosphere than rival JRPGs. A turning point came with the expansion of this brand into the Persona spin-off, which combined demonic combat with a layer of school life, relationships and the passage of the calendar year — a concept that came into full bloom with Persona 3 and Persona 4 on the PlayStation 2. These installments defined the studio's unmistakable visual style, distinctive music and emphasis on themes of growing up and identity, turning Persona into a cultural phenomenon that transcended the JRPG genre. Atlus also gradually built a reputation beyond its main series, for instance with the stylized Catherine, blending puzzle elements with a story about relationships, or spin-offs such as the rhythm game Persona 4: Dancing All Night. Over the course of its history the studio underwent changes in ownership, gradually coming under larger Japanese publishing groups, which gave it a more stable footing and wider distribution abroad. Portable releases such as Persona 4 Golden and later Persona 5 Royal showed how Atlus could keep developing and expanding its games even after their original release. Persona 5 then brought the studio its greatest international popularity to date and set the bar for the next major title, Metaphor: ReFantazio, which carried the proven formula into a fantasy setting.

## Key figures

The long-standing key face of the studio is Katsura Hashino, who served as director on the major Persona titles, including Persona 3, Persona 4 and Persona 5, shaping their characteristic blend of daily routine and combat against demons. His authorial signature, visible in the themes of adolescence, masks and personal identity, is one of the reasons Persona became recognizable even outside the circle of traditional JRPG players. Alongside him, the studio's in-house art and music teams have long contributed to the series' visual identity, and their stylized artwork and distinctive soundtrack work are among the most recognizable elements of the entire Persona brand.

## Today

Atlus today operates as an established studio under the wing of a larger Japanese publishing group and continues to develop its most successful brands, above all Persona and Shin Megami Tensei, including their remasters and expanded editions for new platforms. Its latest major title, Metaphor: ReFantazio, showed that the studio can carry its distinctive style beyond its established modern setting and reach a new generation of players with it. At the same time, Atlus is increasingly focused on a global audience, reflected in the growing number of language versions and faster international releases of its new games. The backing of a larger parent group also allows the studio to develop several major projects in parallel without having to abandon its characteristic, atmosphere- and theme-driven storytelling.
bandai:
Bandai is a Japanese company whose name is inseparably linked with toys, collectible games and licensed entertainment drawn from popular anime and manga brands. In the games industry it made its name above all as a publisher of titles for its own handheld console, the WonderSwan, to which it brought dozens of games built on brands such as Digimon, Rockman, Neon Genesis Evangelion and One Piece. Bandai thus represents a typical example of a Japanese company that managed to fuse its toy and games businesses into one functioning whole and offer players titles closely tied to the popular culture of their time. While many competitors built their gaming success on original brands created directly for video games, Bandai took the opposite path, drawing its strength from already finished and massively popular television and comic-book characters.

## History

Within the games industry, Bandai long positioned itself as a company that built on the strength of its licenses and brands, approaching video games as another outlet for characters it already knew from television screens, toys or collectible cards. A defining step was the launch of the handheld WonderSwan console in the late 1990s, intended to compete with Nintendo's dominant Game Boy and offer Japanese players a cheaper alternative with its own game library. For this platform Bandai published games directly tied to its own and partner franchises — among the first titles were Digital Monster Ver. WonderSwan and Gunpey, a puzzle game whose development involved a Japanese designer famous for his work on Tetris. Shortly afterward came Rockman & Forte: Mirai Kara no Chōsensha and Shinseiki Evangelion: Shito Ikusei, which showed how the company could bring beloved anime and game brands to the new platform, complemented by more original titles such as the horror-tinged Terrors.

Around the turn of the millennium Bandai focused mainly on the Digimon series, which at the time competed for young audiences with the rival Pokémon, and titles such as Digimon Adventure: Anode Tamer and Digimon Adventure 02: Tag Tamers extended the popularity of the digital monsters from the television screen into game form on the WonderSwan. The company continued releasing further licensed games, among them the more original RPG Star Hearts: Hoshi to Daichi no Shisha and the fighting game From TV Animation One Piece: Grand Battle Swan Colosseum, tied to the then still rapidly growing manga phenomenon One Piece, which later became one of Bandai's most successful licenses of all. In the early 21st century Bandai expanded its activities beyond the WonderSwan as well, for instance with the adventure InuYasha: A Feudal Fairy Tale for PlayStation, confirming that the company's licensing portfolio reached far beyond a single console or generation of players. This approach — reacting quickly to currently popular anime and manga series and turning them into games for the widest possible circle of fans — became a hallmark of Bandai even in the years after the WonderSwan had long left the market.

## Today

In 2005 Bandai merged with Namco to form the Bandai Namco conglomerate, which today ranks among the largest game publishers in the world. Under this banner it continues to publish games tied to anime and manga licenses, including long-successful series such as Dragon Ball, Naruto and Tekken, staying true to the strategy it adopted back in the WonderSwan era — linking the gaming experience to the strongest Japanese entertainment brands. The WonderSwan console itself and its game library have today become the domain of collectors and retro enthusiasts, for whom they represent one of the lesser-known yet fascinating chapters of Japanese gaming history at the turn of the millennium.
bethesda-game-studios:
Bethesda Game Studios is an American development studio behind two of the most influential open-world series in modern gaming history — The Elder Scrolls and Fallout. While other studios defined their genres through linear storytelling, Bethesda bet on vast, explorable worlds full of side quests, systemic emergent gameplay and the freedom to do things at your own pace. Morrowind, Oblivion, Skyrim and Fallout 3 became synonymous with open-world RPGs and influenced an entire generation of games that tried to emulate them. The studio is also known for its characteristic habit of re-releasing its own titles again and again on new platforms, which has made Skyrim one of the most ported games of all time.

## History

Bethesda Game Studios is the in-house development studio belonging to publisher Bethesda Softworks, which has roots going back to the 1980s and made its name above all with The Elder Scrolls series. While the series' earliest entries were made under a different studio arrangement, the key turning point came with The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind in the early 2000s — the game showcased the vast, visually unmistakable world of Vvardenfell and set the direction the studio has followed ever since. A few years later Oblivion moved the series onto new consoles and brought improved graphics and more accessible systems, significantly broadening the audience beyond the core of RPG fans. A major expansion of the studio's portfolio came with Fallout 3, through which Bethesda took over the post-apocalyptic Fallout series and carried it into its own open-world style, built on engines also used for Elder Scrolls. The studio's popularity peaked with The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, whose impact on mainstream gaming culture was so strong that the game is still being released on new platforms to this day and has become one of the internet's symbols for the entire genre. It was followed by Fallout 4, which further developed crafting and base-building, and later by the online-focused Fallout 76, which marked a departure from the established single-player formula toward a persistent shared world. In recent years the studio has also ventured into the space RPG Starfield, its first entirely new universe after decades devoted to Elder Scrolls and Fallout.

## Key figures

The studio has long been associated with the name Todd Howard, who serves at Bethesda Game Studios as executive producer and creative director and is the public face behind the direction of both The Elder Scrolls and Fallout series since the days of Morrowind. His approach to open-world design, his emphasis on player freedom and emergent storytelling have become a hallmark of the studio across all its major titles. Howard has also become the public face of the company's presentations at game trade shows, where he regularly unveils the studio's new projects and shapes fan expectations around upcoming games long before their release.

## Today

Bethesda Game Studios is today part of the ZeniMax Media publishing group, which in recent years was acquired by Microsoft, making the studio part of Xbox Game Studios. Despite this change in ownership structure, the studio continues developing its key series — keeping Fallout 76 alive through regular updates and focusing on the further development of Starfield as well as the future of The Elder Scrolls brand. The studio also continues to extend the popularity of the older Skyrim through repeated ports to new platforms, including virtual reality versions. Bethesda Game Studios thus remains one of the most significant creators of open-world RPGs, whose new projects rank among the most anticipated in the entire games industry.
bioware:
BioWare is a Canadian game studio renowned as one of the leading creators of the modern RPG genre, with an emphasis on elaborate storytelling, moral choices, and deeply developed characters. Over the course of its existence, it has been behind the Baldur's Gate, Mass Effect, and Dragon Age series, which rank among the most significant achievements of the genre on both computers and consoles. BioWare has built a reputation as a studio capable of combining vast fantasy or sci-fi worlds with emotionally powerful stories and a dialogue system that gives players a genuine sense of influence over the fate of the characters and the narrative as a whole. This emphasis on story, moral dilemmas, and the deep relationships between the player's character and their companions has become something of a trademark of the entire studio and has inspired numerous other RPG developers around the world.

## History

BioWare was founded by a group of physicians and computer game enthusiasts in the mid-1990s in Edmonton, Canada, who created their first major game based on the rules of Dungeons & Dragons. This title was Baldur's Gate, which revived the computer RPG genre at the end of the 1990s and became both a commercial and critical success, followed by an even more successful sequel, Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn. These games defined the studio's style — sprawling stories, an elaborate party system, and combat based on tabletop RPG rules.

At the start of the 2000s, BioWare expanded its scope with Neverwinter Nights and, notably, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, which brought the studio's proven approach into the Star Wars universe and became one of the most acclaimed titles for the original Xbox. This was followed by Jade Empire, an attempt at a new fantasy IP of its own set in a world inspired by Asian mythology. A pivotal turning point came in 2007 with the release of Mass Effect, a sci-fi saga emphasizing player choice across the entire trilogy, where decisions made in one installment carried over into the sequels. The series became one of the most significant game series of its console generation and is still cited today as an example of a sophisticated fusion of story, characters, and action-RPG gameplay.

At the same time, the studio launched the fantasy series Dragon Age, beginning with Dragon Age: Origins in 2009, which shifted toward a darker and grittier take on a fantasy world compared to BioWare's earlier titles. By this time, BioWare was part of publisher Electronic Arts, under which it remains today, and it continued with further entries in both flagship series, including Dragon Age II, Mass Effect 3, and the expansive Dragon Age: Inquisition. The studio later also released the compilation Mass Effect Legendary Edition, which updated and combined the entire original trilogy for a newer generation of players. More recent titles, such as Dragon Age: The Veilguard, show that even after decades the studio continues trying to keep pace with the changing game market and with the expectations of its longtime fans.

## Key People

BioWare rests on the legacy of its founding creators, who came from a medical background and channeled their passion for tabletop RPGs into computer game form as early as Baldur's Gate. Over the years, a number of creative and game directors have rotated through the individual series, shaping the direction of both Mass Effect and Dragon Age, with the specific composition of the teams changing from project to project.

## Today

BioWare today operates as an Electronic Arts studio and focuses on further developing its two main franchises, Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Following the release of Dragon Age: The Veilguard, the studio faces a mixed reaction from both the player community and the market, but it remains an active development studio with a long-standing tradition and a still-strong fanbase built on its classic titles.
blizzard-entertainment:
Blizzard Entertainment is an American game studio that fundamentally shaped three genres at once with its Warcraft, StarCraft, and Diablo series – real-time strategy, action RPGs, and later also online games such as World of Warcraft. Blizzard is renowned for its emphasis on lengthy development and polished detail, thanks to which its games remain among the most-played titles of their genre even years after release. Besides strategy games and RPGs, the studio was also behind the card game Hearthstone and the team-based shooter Overwatch, demonstrating its ability to successfully enter entirely new game formats as well. For an entire generation of PC gamers, the name Blizzard has been associated with a notion of dependable quality and with the motto "it's done when it's done," which captures the studio's long-standing approach to development at the expense of rapid sequel releases.

## History

Blizzard entered the broader awareness of strategy fans with Warcraft: Orcs & Humans, which pitted the human and orc factions against each other and became the foundation for one of the longest-running game franchises of all. The sequel, Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness, expanded the series' success and paved the way for StarCraft, a sci-fi strategy game that became a phenomenon thanks especially to its well-balanced competitive gameplay and long remained one of the key titles of esports. Alongside its strategy games, Blizzard also developed the action-RPG series Diablo, whose subsequent installments defined the genre of loot collecting and endless character progression. The turn of the millennium and the following years brought the expansion Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos, whose story and factions later became the basis for the massively multiplayer game World of Warcraft, followed by the sequel StarCraft II: Wings of Liberty, which showed that the studio could successfully carry its classic franchises into a new generation of players and a modern online environment. Blizzard operated during this time as part of a publishing group that underwent several changes in ownership structure without significantly disrupting the direction of its flagship series. Diablo III was released first on computers and later brought to consoles, including PlayStation 3, demonstrating the studio's effort to reach players beyond the traditional PC platform. In subsequent years, the studio expanded its portfolio with the card game Hearthstone and the team-based shooter Overwatch, cementing its position as one of the most significant developers of its era, and went on to release the complete Diablo III: Eternal Collection package on Switch, followed by the entirely new installment Diablo IV on PlayStation 5 and PC.

## Key People

Blizzard Entertainment has long been associated with the names of its founders, who were behind the studio's first titles and shaped its approach to lengthy, detail-focused development. This approach became part of the studio's corporate culture and was reflected in Blizzard's willingness to delay a game's release by months or years if the result did not meet its own quality standards. The specific roles of individual creators changed over the decades as the studio grew and its leadership went through changes, and a number of people from the original team later left to found their own studios continuing in a similar style of game.

## Today

Blizzard Entertainment remains an active studio today and continues to develop and support its key franchises, including the latest installments of the Diablo series, the card game Hearthstone, and the shooter Overwatch. The studio remains part of a larger publishing group and continues to be among the most recognized names associated with the strategy, action-RPG, and online multiplayer genres, while still relying on the long-term support of its classic Warcraft, StarCraft, and Diablo series, which shaped entire decades of the game industry.
bullfrog-productions:
Bullfrog Productions was a British game studio that, in the 1990s, was among the most imaginative creators in the simulation and strategy genre. It became famous for games such as Populous, Syndicate, Theme Park, and Dungeon Keeper – titles that offered an unusual top-down perspective, playful graphics, and a sense of dark humor. Bullfrog was one of the studios that co-created the so-called "god game" genre, meaning games where the player does not control a single character but instead runs an entire world or civilization from the position of an almost divine entity. For many players on DOS and early Windows, Bullfrog was synonymous with originality and experimentation, unafraid to combine strategy, simulation, and humor in a single package. The studio built a reputation for daring to take risks with unconventional game concepts at a time when most of the competition relied on established genres, and it was precisely this boldness that made it one of the most influential brands of the 1990s computer game industry.

## History

The studio was founded in the United Kingdom, and its breakthrough came with Populous, which offered players the role of a deity shaping the landscape and leading their followers against an enemy. This title helped define an entire genre and paved the way for further projects such as Powermonger or the military strategy game Syndicate, praised for its dark cyberpunk-future atmosphere. In the mid-1990s, Bullfrog released Magic Carpet and Theme Park, a game about building an amusement park that showed the studio was able to combine economic simulation with a lighthearted tone. The pinnacle of its output came with Dungeon Keeper, which turned the classic fantasy formula on its head by having the player build and defend an underground dungeon, and Theme Hospital, a satirical hospital simulation. In the 1990s, the studio was part of publisher Electronic Arts, under whose wing later titles were also created, including Populous: The Beginning, a return to the original series in the form of a full-fledged three-dimensional strategy game. Versions of some games also made their way to consoles and unusual platforms – for example, Syndicate and Theme Park were released on the 3DO, and Magic Carpet even appeared in a version adapted for the VFX1 headset, illustrating just how experimental Bullfrog's approach to distributing its games was. Over time, however, key creators began leaving to found their own studios and develop similar game concepts elsewhere, which led to the fragmentation of the original team and the gradual decline of the Bullfrog brand as an independent studio within the Electronic Arts structure.

## Key People

The studio was founded by Peter Molyneux, one of the most distinctive figures in the British game industry, known for his emphasis on simulating living systems and for his ambitious game design. His approach to building worlds and mechanics, in which the player intervenes in events more as an indirect ruler than as a directly controlled character, shaped the direction of Bullfrog throughout its existence. Around Molyneux, a team of designers and programmers formed within Bullfrog who turned his concepts into working games, and many of them went on to contribute to further projects within the British game scene after his departure.

## Today

Bullfrog Productions as an active development studio gradually ceased to exist after key people left to found new projects and Electronic Arts completed the wind-down of the studio. Bullfrog's legacy, however, lives on in the simulation and strategy genres that its titles helped define, and many later games openly cite the ideas of Populous, Dungeon Keeper, or Theme Park as their inspiration. Brands such as Theme Hospital and Dungeon Keeper have also received modern remasters and re-releases, allowing even players who never experienced the original DOS games to discover Bullfrog's playful style.
bungie:
Bungie is one of those studios whose name became synonymous with an entire gaming platform — without Halo, the early history of Xbox would look completely different. It started out as a small independent team focused on Macintosh and gradually rose to become one of the most influential developers of action games of all time. Along the way it underwent a dramatic transformation: from an independent studio it became part of Microsoft, only to later become independent again and eventually end up under the wing of Sony. Its legacy, however, remains firmly tied to two great series that shaped the entire genre of first-person shooters and online multiplayer worlds alike — Halo and Destiny.

## History

Bungie went through a long journey before it became a company associated with Xbox. It first focused on games for Macintosh and smaller titles, until the breakthrough came with the strategy series Myth, which showed that the studio could build distinctive game worlds and sophisticated multiplayer experiences. The real turning point, though, was the project Halo: Combat Evolved. The game, originally developed as a title for computers, ultimately became the flagship launch title of the first Xbox console and played a crucial role in helping Microsoft establish itself in the game console market. Shortly before Halo's release, Microsoft acquired Bungie, turning the studio into an internal division tied almost exclusively to a single platform and a single brand. More Halo installments followed, expanding the story, the multiplayer, and the technical capabilities of the engine, and cementing the series' position as one of the pillars of the Xbox ecosystem. After years of intensive work on Halo, Bungie split from Microsoft in 2007 and became independent again, though it continued collaborating on Halo for some time afterward. The studio then set itself a new goal — to build its own universe outside of Halo. The result was Destiny, an online shooter combining elements of MMO, RPG, and classic action, which Bungie published in partnership with publisher Activision. After that partnership ended, the studio went its own way with the sequel Destiny 2 and further development of the online service as a long-term project. Since its release, Destiny 2 has evolved through large paid expansions that gradually rewrote the game's map and even changed its core systems, turning it into a live service rather than a one-and-done release. This model, where a game keeps growing for years after launch, became the defining trait of the second half of the studio's history and set Bungie apart from its earlier identity as a creator of self-contained stories from the Halo era.

## Key People

Among the people most often associated with Bungie is Jason Jones, one of the studio's founders, who was behind its early projects, including the Myth series, and later the very concept of Halo itself. Alongside him, the studio's early era is also tied to the name of Alex Seropian, another of its founding members. Marcus Lehto also played a long-term role in shaping the Halo series, serving as art director behind the visual look of the space soldier Master Chief, as did Joseph Staten, who for many years oversaw the series' narrative and writing. The precise personnel changes at the studio in later years, especially around the transition to Destiny, shifted so much over time that reliably documenting every additional name would go beyond the scope of this text.

## Today

Today Bungie is an independent studio focused on the long-term development of Destiny 2 as a live service, with regular seasonal updates and larger expansions that gradually change the game world and its story. The studio has maintained its own production team and game engine throughout, one it originally built for Halo. In recent years Bungie became part of Sony, placing it among the key studios in the Japanese console maker's portfolio, though it continues to maintain its own identity, brand, and direction outside the traditional single-platform exclusives. Destiny 2 remains its main, and practically only, actively developed title, around which the vast majority of the studio's work is now focused.
cd-projekt-red:
CD Projekt RED is a Polish game studio that grew from a local developer into one of the most significant game creators in the world. It was founded as the development arm of the distribution and publishing company CD Projekt, and built its reputation on The Witcher series, loosely based on the books of Polish writer Andrzej Sapkowski. The studio is known for its ambitious approach to storytelling, morally ambiguous player choices, and expansive open worlds, as well as for its willingness to go against established practices of the games business, for example by refusing DRM protection. The pinnacle of its work so far is The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, one of the most acclaimed RPGs ever made, which was followed by a bold shift toward the sci-fi world of Cyberpunk 2077. In a relatively short time, CD Projekt RED managed to achieve what many European studios never did — establishing itself on the global market with two completely different, yet equally strong, brands.

## History

CD Projekt RED was founded as the development branch of the Polish company CD Projekt, which had previously focused mainly on distributing and localizing foreign games for the Polish market. The studio's first major project was the action RPG The Witcher, built on the literary work of Andrzej Sapkowski, which opened the door for the studio onto the international scene. Its success was cemented by the sequel The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings, which placed greater emphasis on branching storylines and decisions with long-term consequences. The turning-point title became The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — a sprawling open-world RPG initially released for PC and consoles of that era, and later also for Nintendo Switch. The game received extraordinarily positive reception and pushed CD Projekt RED into the world's top tier of game development. In the meantime, the studio also built its own distribution platform, GOG.com, focused on DRM-free games, and expanded The Witcher universe with the card game Gwent and the story spin-off Thronebreaker. Its next big step was a shift away from fantasy toward the sci-fi genre with Cyberpunk 2077, set in the dystopian Night City. Its 2020 release was accompanied by extensive technical problems, especially on older-generation consoles, which led to significant media pressure and the game's temporary removal from one storefront. The studio subsequently spent a long time fixing and expanding the game, thanks to which its reputation gradually improved considerably. This turnaround is often cited today as an example that even after a troubled launch, a game's — and an entire studio's — reputation can be rebuilt through sustained work and communication with players.

## Key People

We deliberately avoid naming specific founders and lead creators of the studio to avoid inaccuracies — but it can be said that CD Projekt RED benefited from the start from its close ties to its parent company CD Projekt, which allowed it to invest long-term in its own ambitious projects even during periods when other European studios struggled to do so. This connection between a development studio and its parent distribution and publishing company is one of the traits that has long set the Polish game scene apart from many other European countries.

## Today

CD Projekt RED today ranks among the leading European game studios and continues to develop both of its key brands. After fixing Cyberpunk 2077, including the release of an expansion and versions for newer consoles, the game arrived on Nintendo Switch 2 in the form of Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition. At the same time, the studio is working on further installments of both series for a new generation of players. The studio publicly presents the lessons learned from the demanding development and launch of Cyberpunk 2077 as something it wants to carry into its internal processes for its next major projects, so that a similarly turbulent start doesn't happen again.
codemasters:
Codemasters is a British studio whose name is still practically synonymous with racing games on PC and consoles. From eight-bit computers through the NES and SNES to today's PlayStation and Xbox, the company has gone through several genre phases, but it was motorsport simulations and arcade racers that earned it its most lasting reputation. Series like Colin McRae Rally, TOCA, and later DiRT and the official Formula 1 games made Codemasters a benchmark brand for anyone looking for a believable sense of driving on screen, and their influence on the racing genre is still visible today across the entire industry, including how surface physics and vehicle behavior are modeled in games today. Throughout, the studio has retained the ability to switch between a strictly simulation-focused and a lighter arcade approach depending on which title it was developing at the time.

## History

Codemasters was founded in Britain in the 1980s during the era of home eight-bit computers, and in its early years was among the prolific publishers of accessible arcade games for the wide range of British home computers of the time. The company reached wider international awareness thanks to the Micro Machines series, which brought the concept of racing with miniature model cars to game consoles — the first installment appeared on the NES in 1991, was later followed by a reworked version for the SNES, and became one of the beloved local multiplayer titles of its generation, prized above all for its clever, creative tracks.

In the second half of the 1990s, Codemasters turned decisively toward realistic motorsport simulations. TOCA Touring Car Championship from 1998 brought the atmosphere of touring car circuit racing to PC and set a high standard for driving physics; a year later the studio followed up with the rallycross series Colin McRae Rally, named after the real-life world rally champion. Thanks to its authentic sense of driving and the license of a real driver, the series became one of the most successful rally brands in video game history and continued after 2000 with installments such as Colin McRae Rally 2.0, which was also released on the consoles of the time.

In the following decade, the studio expanded its portfolio with the DiRT series; the looser, more arcade-focused DiRT 3 from 2011 was followed in 2015 by the tougher, more simulation-focused DiRT Rally, praised especially by hardcore rally fans for its emphasis on physics, terrain, and demanding tracks. Codemasters also gradually took over the Formula 1 license, under which it still publishes the official annual game of the series with the current season, tracks, and drivers, and expanded DiRT with the spin-off Dirt 5, with an even stronger emphasis on a more fun, more accessible, and more visually stylized take on racing. This gave the studio a presence in two distinct segments of the motorsport genre at once — on one side faithful rally simulation, and on the other accessible arcade racing and the licensed Formula series.

## Today

In recent years Codemasters has become part of a larger publishing conglomerate focused on sports and motorsport games, but its teams continue to develop titles both under their own name and under the EA Sports brand. The annual release of the official Formula 1 game and the continuation of the DiRT and Colin McRae series remain the core of the studio's output, and even after decades in existence it retains a reputation as a leading specialist in the motorsport and racing genre, comparable to only a handful of other studios in the world. Even after moving under a larger publishing group, the Codemasters brand remains visible on game boxes, and for fans of motorsport simulations it still stands as a guarantee of a certain craft quality and authenticity that the company has been building since its earliest rally titles.
criterion-games:
Criterion Games is a British development studio that made its name chiefly with the Burnout racing series, renowned for its emphasis on adrenaline-fuelled speed, spectacular crashes, and an arcade approach to driving rather than simulation-grade precision. The studio gradually built a reputation as one of the most experienced teams in the arcade racing genre, and its technology and design philosophy later influenced other major franchises when Criterion took over development of entries in the Need for Speed series. Besides racing games, the studio was also behind the RenderWare technology engine, which for a time was widely used across the games industry, from smaller developers to major publishers looking for a ready-made solution for three-dimensional graphics and physics.

## History

Criterion Games emerged as the development arm of Criterion Software, a company originally known mainly for its game-development technology and middleware, including the aforementioned RenderWare engine. The studio began releasing its own games at the start of the 21st century, and with the very first entry in the Burnout series on PlayStation 2 it showed where its work would head: fast arcade racing built around spectacular vehicle destruction. The series continued to grow through further entries, which gradually refined the slow-motion crash system and added new game modes.

A turning point came with Burnout 3: Takedown, which won broad attention from both players and critics for its aggressive yet entertaining take on on-track combat, where taking down rivals mattered just as much as the finish line itself. The studio then briefly stepped away from racing with the action shooter Black, which showed that Criterion could handle environmental destruction outside the car genre too, before returning to its tried-and-tested formula with Burnout Dominator. Burnout Paradise followed, marking the studio's first departure from traditional linear tracks in favour of a connected open city that players could freely drive around, with no menus or loading screens between races. During the series' development, Criterion Games became part of publisher Electronic Arts, which later put the studio's arcade racing expertise to use for another major franchise.

After the release of Burnout Paradise, the studio became increasingly involved in developing the Need for Speed series, delivering entries such as Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit, which combined Burnout-style speed with chases between police and drivers, as well as a portable version of Need for Speed: Most Wanted for the Vita console. Criterion Games thus gradually became one of the key teams keeping the Need for Speed series alive under the Electronic Arts banner, while its own Burnout brand faded into the background for a while. The original game was eventually revisited with Burnout Paradise Remastered, which brought the classic title to a newer console generation, and a few years later the studio once again contributed to the Need for Speed series with Need for Speed Unbound, which combined a realistic setting with striking comic-book-style visuals.

## Today

Today Criterion Games operates as part of Electronic Arts and remains long-term involved in developing and supporting the Need for Speed series, including more recent entries like Need for Speed Unbound. The studio has kept its reputation as a team specialising in arcade racing with an emphasis on speed and visual spectacle, even though its own Burnout brand hasn't received a new entry in recent years and exists mainly in the form of a remastered version of an older title. Among fans of both Need for Speed and Burnout, Criterion Games remains associated above all with a sense of speed and spectacular, almost cinematic crashes, which have been the hallmark of its work ever since its earliest entries in the early 2000s.
crystal-dynamics:
Crystal Dynamics is an American development studio whose history stretches back to the early days of the 3DO and which gradually rose to become a key creator of one of the best-known action-adventure series in video game history — Tomb Raider. The studio's journey from experimental titles for what was then a new and short-lived games system to the globally successful reboot of the iconic archaeologist Lara Croft ranks among the more remarkable stories of survival and reinvention in the games industry. Crystal Dynamics was also, for a long time, behind the darker Legacy of Kain series, through which it built a reputation as a studio with a feel for atmospheric storytelling and richly crafted game worlds.

## History

Crystal Dynamics was founded at the start of the 1990s, and its earliest steps were closely tied to the 3DO console, for which it created several launch and early titles. These included the racing game Crash 'n Burn, the action title Total Eclipse, a port of the fighting game Samurai Shodown, and the vehicular shooter Off-World Interceptor. These games were meant to showcase the technical capabilities of what was then a new games system, one built around CD media and more powerful 3D graphics than players were used to from the previous generation of consoles and home computers. This early phase shaped the studio into a team capable of working on technically demanding projects for what was then cutting-edge hardware, even though the 3DO platform itself never gained lasting traction on the market and folded fairly quickly. The move to the next console generation also brought a genre shift — in 1995 the studio released Gex, a platformer starring a gecko as its main character, which gradually became one of Crystal Dynamics' founding franchises on other platforms and went on to receive its own sequels.

A major turning point came with the Legacy of Kain series, a dark action-adventure set in a gothic world of vampires and demons, which the studio carried through several entries including Soul Reaver 2 and Legacy of Kain: Defiance on PS2. This series built a strong cult following thanks to its storytelling, striking voice performances, and elaborate mythology that grew steadily from one entry to the next, and to this day is cited by many players as one of the best-written game series of its era. Alongside its own franchises, the studio was during this period also involved in developing and publishing other titles for the consoles of the day, which helped it maintain a stable position within a larger publishing portfolio.

The truly defining moment for the whole studio, however, came in 2013 with the reboot of the Tomb Raider series, which completely reimagined Lara Croft as a character and shifted the game's overall tone toward a rawer, more realistic story of survival on a mysterious island. The reboot was received very positively by both critics and players and set the franchise's new direction for years to come. Its success was confirmed by the sequel Rise of the Tomb Raider, released for Xbox One, which further developed the gameplay systems, exploration possibilities, and storytelling, cementing Crystal Dynamics' position as the main custodian of the Tomb Raider brand throughout the entire rebooted trilogy.

## Today

To this day, Crystal Dynamics remains primarily associated with the Tomb Raider series, in whose future direction it continues to play a role, in varying degrees, even after the release of the rebooted trilogy — whether through direct development or oversight of the franchise's legacy. Over the years the studio has undergone several changes of ownership within larger publishing groups, which is fairly common for long-running development studios of this scale, and it remains an established name on the American games scene with a rich history stretching back to the earliest days of 3D console gaming and its first experimental platforms.
dice:
DICE, a Swedish studio based in Stockholm, is a name inseparably tied to the Battlefield series and to the large-scale multiplayer battles that have defined the war-action genre on PCs and consoles since the start of the 21st century. While the competition long relied on linear campaigns, DICE bet on sprawling battlefields, vehicles, and environmental destruction, creating a counterpart to the Call of Duty series. For genre fans, the studio is synonymous with massive online battles where the outcome is decided by teamwork and large-scale tactics rather than shooting mechanics alone, and where players learn to use terrain, vehicles, and collapsed buildings as part of their own strategy.

## History

The studio Digital Illusions, later renamed Digital Illusions CE and known by the abbreviation DICE, was founded in Sweden in the early 1990s and in its first years worked across various genres, including racing and sports games, before its direction changed fundamentally with the arrival of the Battlefield series. DICE entered the war genre precisely through this series, whose first major entry, Battlefield 1942, placed players in the Second World War and combined infantry, vehicles, and aircraft on a single map at a scale that had no equal on PCs at the time. The game became one of the first truly popular multiplayer titles built around large vehicle battles and laid the foundation for the studio's entire design philosophy. Battlefield Vietnam and Battlefield 2 followed, expanding the class and commander-role system, adding more sophisticated team communication, and cementing the series' position as the main rival to Call of Duty in the multiplayer shooter segment.

The move to the then-current console generation brought Battlefield: Bad Company 2, which popularised destructible environments and, for the first time, brought the series closer to a wider console audience. Battlefield 3 then introduced the studio's own Frostbite technology, which enabled more realistic graphics, more extensive environmental destruction, and more advanced sound and lighting simulation, and became the backbone of later entries as well as a number of other Electronic Arts games outside the Battlefield series. Battlefield 4 deepened this direction further, despite a rocky launch marred by technical problems.

Battlefield 1, released in 2016, unexpectedly moved the series to the First World War, and through its combination of an unusual historical period, strong atmosphere, and an extensive multi-character campaign, it became one of the series' most commercially successful entries. Battlefield V then returned to the Second World War with an emphasis on smaller, more tactical engagements, more elaborate cover destruction, and live services in the form of seasonal content, reflecting the broader trend in online shooters of the time, where games sought to retain players long-term through regular updates rather than a one-off release.

## Today

DICE has been part of publisher Electronic Arts since 2006 and remains the lead studio responsible for the Battlefield series, on whose development it today often collaborates with other internal EA teams spread around the world, which has become the standard model for developing the series' major games. Even after more than two decades, the Battlefield brand retains its position as one of the main pillars of the large-scale online war-game genre, and the Frostbite technology the studio developed remains one of the publisher's key tools, used for other franchises as well. For many players, the name DICE remains, to this day, above all a guarantee of sprawling battlefields and destruction, on which the series' multiplayer has been built from the very beginning.
dma-design:
DMA Design was a Scottish studio from Dundee that managed to come up with two utterly different yet equally groundbreaking ideas — the puzzle game Lemmings and the open-world crime game Grand Theft Auto. While Lemmings, in which tiny green-haired creatures had to be saved from certain doom using a set of simple commands, became a phenomenon ported to virtually every platform of the early nineties, Grand Theft Auto a few years later sparked one of the biggest controversies in video game history while laying the foundation for one of the most commercially successful gaming franchises of all time. DMA Design itself later evolved into Rockstar North, the studio that still develops GTA today.

## History

DMA Design was founded in Dundee, Scotland, in the second half of the 1980s, initially focusing on games for home computers such as the Commodore 64 and Amiga. True worldwide success came only with Lemmings (1991) — a game in which the player doesn't control a single character but a horde of tiny creatures marching toward doom, who must be assigned tasks like digging, building, or blocking their path in order to reach safety. The game became one of the biggest hits of its era and was ported to almost everything that existed at the time — from the Amiga and DOS through the Sega Mega Drive and Sega Master System to the CD-i console — finding its own audience on every platform.

After the success of Lemmings, DMA Design moved on to more experimental projects before releasing, in 1997, a game that made the studio famous in a completely different way — Grand Theft Auto. The top-down view, an open city, and the ability to play as a criminal sparked a wave of moral panic in the media and among politicians, which, paradoxically, only added to the game's popularity. The sequel Grand Theft Auto 2 (1999) developed the concept further and moved it to a fictional futuristic city. During this period the studio was acquired by the American publisher Take-Two Interactive, which saw enormous commercial potential in DMA Design. The real turning point came with Grand Theft Auto III (2001) on the PlayStation 2 — by moving to a fully three-dimensional open world, the game defined the genre for the next two decades and propelled both the series and the entire studio into the most prominent names in the games industry. In 2002, DMA Design was renamed Rockstar North and became the core of the Rockstar Games publishing label.

## Key People

The studio was founded by David Jones, a programmer and designer who also stood behind the original concept of Lemmings and was one of the people who turned DMA Design from a small Scottish team into a name with worldwide reach.
