Jones left the company back in the 1990s, before the renaming to Rockstar North, and founded his own development studio, where he continued making games outside of Take-Two's umbrella. After his departure, creative leadership was taken over by other longtime team members who had been present at the birth of Grand Theft Auto and who steered the studio through the turbulent late nineties all the way to the renaming as Rockstar North, under which the company still operates today.

## Today

The former DMA Design now operates as Rockstar North, one of the key studios of the Rockstar Games publishing label, and remains the principal architect of the Grand Theft Auto series as well as other major projects from the company. The original DMA Design name may have disappeared from game boxes as early as the early 2000s, but its legacy lives on in every new GTA installment and in the very DNA of the studio, which is still based in Scotland. Meanwhile, the Lemmings brand has passed to other owners and returns to new players mainly through occasional remakes and mobile versions, while the name DMA Design remains just a historical chapter in the family tree of one of the most influential game studios of today.
electronic-arts:
Electronic Arts ranks among the most influential and, at the same time, most controversial companies in the history of video games. From a small publisher that, in the era of home computers, promoted its authors as artists comparable to musicians or filmmakers, it grew into a giant whose sports and racing series accompanied entire generations of players. The EA name is tied to titles like FIFA, Need for Speed, and Road Rash, and the company's emphasis on licensed sports and realistic presentation helped define what mainstream entertainment on consoles and computers looks like. Unlike studios built around a single strong brand, EA from the very beginning built the image of a publisher with a broad portfolio of genres, able to successfully serve both simulation fans and the mass sports market.

## History

Electronic Arts was founded in the early 1980s as a publisher focused on home computers, at a time when the market was only just learning to distinguish between games as a crafted product and games as an authored work. From the outset, the company positioned itself as a business that valued its creators and presented them to the public much the way music labels present their artists. In the second half of the 1980s, EA focused on simulators and strategy games for DOS, including the submarine simulation 688 Attack Sub and the flight training program Chuck Yeager's Advanced Flight Trainer, which demonstrated technical precision and an interest in realistic simulations.

The first half of the 1990s proved pivotal, as EA expanded its portfolio with racing and sports games that became its main financial pillar for decades to come. The brutal motorcycle series Road Rash was born, available on the Sega Mega Drive and the 3DO, where the sequels Road Rash II and Road Rash 3 developed the concept of illegal, fight-filled street races further. In 1994 the first installment of FIFA International Soccer was released, kicking off the longest-running sports game series ever and becoming the foundation on which EA built its sports business for decades to come.

At the end of the decade, EA also bet on road racing with licensed cars through the Need for Speed series, where titles like Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit and Need for Speed: Porsche Unleashed combined arcade fun with carefully crafted models of real cars, built for computers running Windows 9x, which at the time was becoming the standard platform for gaming. This model — annual sports editions supplemented by strong racing and action brands — became the template for how the company operated in the following decades as well, as EA gradually absorbed a number of other studios worldwide through acquisitions and built one of the largest game publishers in the world.

## Key People

In its early days, the company was shaped by Trip Hawkins, who came up with the concept of presenting game developers as recognized authors and was behind EA's launch as a publisher with a distinctive marketing identity. His vision of positioning games as a cultural product comparable to music or film influenced how the company communicated with its customers for decades to come.

## Today

Electronic Arts is today among the largest game publishers in the world, and its series such as FIFA (now called EA Sports FC), Need for Speed, and Battlefield remain very commercially successful. In recent years the company has focused primarily on live services, online multiplayer, and long-term supported sports titles, continuing the strategy it set out already in the 1990s. Original series such as Road Rash, meanwhile, have remained preserved in their retro form and today serve mainly as a reminder of the time when EA was still building its reputation as a dominant publisher of sports and racing games.
fromsoftware:
FromSoftware is a Japanese studio that transformed from a maker of mech simulators and bone-chilling action RPGs into one of the most influential game design creators of the last fifteen years. Today the studio's name is inseparably tied to the Souls series and to the word derived from it — soulslike, a genre defined by a measured, uncompromising, yet fair combat system. But before FromSoftware discovered this formula, it went through a long journey from the early King's Field games, through the techno-action Armored Core series, to the dark Demon's Souls, which kicked off one of the most distinctive waves in modern gaming history.

## History

The studio was founded in Tokyo in the mid-1980s and spent its first era experimenting with various genres, among which the mech action series Armored Core and the early 3D RPG King's Field stood out, earning the studio a reputation as a creator of dense, technically demanding worlds. It was precisely this experience with a relentless, slow, and deliberate combat pace that later became the foundation for the studio's greatest success.

The turning point was 2009 and Demon's Souls for the PlayStation 3 — a game that combined a dark atmosphere, minimalist storytelling, and an uncompromising yet fair combat system in a form no one else offered at the time. The follow-up Dark Souls (2011) expanded the formula into a more interconnected, open world and launched a series that would go on to receive the sequels Dark Souls II and Dark Souls III. Meanwhile, in 2015 FromSoftware released Bloodborne, a PlayStation 4 exclusive that, with its gothic horror aesthetic and faster combat, showed that the studio was able to vary its formula.

The next milestone was Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice (2019), which abandoned the branching character-building system in favor of a more direct, parry-based combat system set in feudal Japan. The pinnacle of the studio's work to date became Elden Ring (2022), an open world created in collaboration with fantasy author George R. R. Martin, which multiplied the series' reach far beyond its existing player base and became one of the most successful titles of its generation. In 2014, FromSoftware came under the wing of the Japanese publishing and media conglomerate Kadokawa, which gave the studio a stable foundation for further growth.

## Key People

The face of the studio's modern era is undoubtedly **Hidetaka Miyazaki**, director of Demon's Souls, Dark Souls, Bloodborne, Sekiro, and Elden Ring, who gradually worked his way up to the position of FromSoftware's president and is considered one of the most distinctive game creators of today. The studio was founded by **Naotoshi Zin**, who was there at its creation, back when FromSoftware worked in genres completely different from the action RPGs it is famous for today.

## Today

Even in 2026, FromSoftware remains one of the most closely watched studios in the world, and the soulslike formula it helped create has influenced the entire games industry — dozens of other studios today claim its legacy. The studio remains part of the Kadokawa conglomerate and continues developing the world of Elden Ring along with other projects, and even after years of success it maintains its reputation as a creator that has never sacrificed its demanding yet fair gameplay for the sake of simplifying things for a broader audience.
hudson-soft:
Hudson Soft was a Japanese development and publishing studio from Sapporo that ranked among the pioneers of the home gaming industry, and its name is still tied above all to the Bomberman series. The company also co-created the PC Engine console together with the electronics giant NEC, and in the nineties and the early two-thousands it was one of the most prolific Japanese studios of all — developing its own brands such as Adventure Island and Bomberman while also becoming a key external partner for Nintendo on the Mario Party series. For the generation of players who grew up with the NES, Super Nintendo, Game Boy Advance and GameCube, Hudson Soft is synonymous with accessible, party-style, cooperative games that could be played with the whole family or a group of friends around a single television.

## History

Hudson Soft was founded in the early seventies as a small company dealing in computer software and radio broadcasting, and it gradually shifted toward video games, first on Japanese home computers and later on game consoles. A turning point came with its collaboration with the electronics company NEC on the development of the PC Engine console, launched in Japan in the mid-eighties — Hudson Soft became one of its main supporters and game suppliers, which helped the platform build a strong position on the domestic market despite its limited success abroad under the name TurboGrafx-16. In the same period the studio launched the Bomberman series, whose simple yet immensely addictive concept of explosive mazes and multiplayer duels became one of the longest-running brands in the entire industry, along with the Adventure Island series, a popular platformer also available on the NES and later on handhelds. For the PC Engine console itself, Hudson Soft even created its own mascot character, the cave boy Bonk, who became one of the faces of the platform much as Sonic represented Sega or Mario represented Nintendo.

In the nineties Hudson Soft expanded its activities to handhelds as well, collaborating on a number of titles for the Game Boy and Virtual Boy, including action puzzle games like Panic Bomber or the localization of the Pokémon Trading Card Game for the Game Boy Color. A major shift came with the turn of the millennium, when the studio became the lead developer of the Mario Party series for the Nintendo GameCube and later for the Nintendo DS and Wii — meaning it stood behind one of the most successful party-game concepts ever, even though it was an intellectual property owned by Nintendo rather than the studio's own. At the same time, Hudson Soft kept developing its own IP, for instance Bomberman spin-offs for the Game Boy Advance such as Bomberman Tournament, which added new game modes and expanded the multiplayer options.

The ongoing consolidation of the Japanese gaming market meant that, over the course of the two-thousands, Konami built up a significant stake in the studio and gradually acquired Hudson Soft outright. After several years of operating as a subsidiary, the studio was formally merged into Konami in 2012 and ceased to exist as an independent brand, closing the nearly forty-year history of one of the oldest Japanese game publishers.

## Today

Hudson Soft as an independent studio ceased to exist when it was absorbed into Konami. Its best-known brand, Bomberman, however lives on under the Konami banner, which regularly releases new entries and remasters for current consoles, while the legacy of its collaboration on the Mario Party series continues in the hands of Nintendo and its other development partners. The name Hudson Soft today mainly remains a memory of an era when Japanese studios were still finding the rules of the genres that continue to shape family and party games to this day.
id-software:
id Software is an American studio that gave birth to the first-person shooter genre and, for many years, determined the direction the action game would take. The name is tied to the trio of Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Quake — games that progressively defined what an FPS even is, while also pushing the limits of what the hardware of the day could do. For retro players id Software is synonymous with the shareware revolution of the nineties, modem multiplayer, and technology engines that dozens of other companies licensed from the studio. Few studios have shaped the development of the entire games industry as fundamentally as this crew of programmers from Texas.

## History

id Software was founded in the early nineties in Texas by a group of people who met while working at the software company Softdisk. After leaving, they founded their own studio, and its very first years showed where it was headed — the platformer series Commander Keen proved that the hardware limits of the PC could be circumvented with clever programming. The turning point was 1992 and Wolfenstein 3D, a game that popularized the first-person perspective and spread across the world through the shareware model.

A year later came Doom, a title that changed perceptions of violence and atmosphere in computer games and popularized both networked multiplayer and modding — players modified the engine and built their own levels before that was common practice. Doom II (1994) expanded the content and the fan base further. In 1996 Quake arrived, pushing the genre into full 3D graphics and introducing online multiplayer over the internet, which made it one of the pillars of the nascent esports scene. The sequels Quake II and Quake III Arena cemented the studio's reputation as a technology leader.

After the turn of the millennium the release pace slowed, but id Software remained an engine of technological innovation — Doom 3 (2004) showcased the power of a new engine built on dynamic lighting. In 2009 the studio was bought by ZeniMax Media, the parent company of Bethesda, and id became part of a larger publishing group. The reboot of the series in the form of Doom (2016) and its sequel Doom Eternal (2020) showed that, even decades later, the studio could still define what fast, brutal action should look like. Along with the rest of ZeniMax, id Software became part of Microsoft in 2021.

## Key people

The founding foursome consisted of programmer **John Carmack**, level designer and game visionary **John Romero**, artist **Adrian Carmack** and designer **Tom Hall**. John Carmack is considered one of the most influential programmers in the history of games — his technical solutions for Wolfenstein, Doom and Quake pushed the limits of what computers of the time could do, and he later moved on to research in virtual reality. John Romero was the studio's public face and the driving force behind the game design of its early titles, though he left the studio in the mid-nineties. Adrian Carmack was responsible for the dark visual style of the classic games.

## Today

id Software today operates as an internal studio under Bethesda, and thus within Microsoft, focusing primarily on the Doom series. After the successful 2016 reboot and the sequel Doom Eternal, the studio continues to develop the brand with further entries and expansions, while maintaining its reputation as one of the most technologically advanced developers of action games. Although the founding generation has long since left the studio, the legacy of Wolfenstein, Doom and Quake remains alive — not only through modern sequels, but also through an active community that still creates its own levels and mods for the original titles.
insomniac-games:
Insomniac Games is one of the most stable and longest-running studios tied exclusively to a single console family — from the very first PlayStation to the PS5, it has made games solely for Sony. Over three decades of existence it has built a reputation as a studio that can combine technical precision with irreverent humor and inventive level design. It first made its name with the Spyro the Dragon series, then even more prominently with the action series Ratchet & Clank, one of the longest-running exclusive PlayStation brands. In recent years the studio has turned into one of the key creators of major licensed titles, taking over development of the Spider-Man games. Insomniac is today part of Sony, and its games rank among the platform's technological and commercial flagships. Unlike studios that built their existence around a single genre specialization, Insomniac has repeatedly jumped between platformers, action-adventures, sci-fi shooters and large-scale superhero games without losing its recognizable sense of pace and playfulness.

## History

The studio was founded in the first half of the nineties, and its growth was helped by a close relationship with Sony right from the launch of the first PlayStation console. Its breakthrough was the platformer Spyro the Dragon, thanks to which Insomniac became one of the platform's most trusted external developers. After moving to the PlayStation 2, the studio came up with its own new brand, Ratchet & Clank, combining an action platformer with weapons full of humor and inventiveness — the series subsequently became one of the longest-maintained PlayStation exclusives and carried through the PS2, PS3, PS4 and PS5 generations alongside the console. At the same time the studio experimented outside its established series as well: on the PS3 it launched the sci-fi shooter Resistance: Fall of Man, later tried multiplatform projects too, and on the Xbox One released the stylized open-world shooter Sunset Overdrive. A turning point came when it moved under Sony's wing as an internal studio, after which Insomniac took charge of developing games under the Marvel's Spider-Man license. These titles showed that the studio could handle not only its own brands but also major film licenses on a large scale, and they cemented its position among PlayStation's top internal studios. Interestingly, Insomniac has managed to maintain a relatively regular release rhythm throughout its history — while many other large studios leave gaps of many years between titles, Insomniac has managed to develop several series in parallel and move smoothly between console generations without having to dramatically restructure its studios or fundamentally change its development direction.

## Key people

We would rather not list the specific names of the studio's founders and key creative figures here, so as not to risk inaccuracy — the history of Insomniac Games has nevertheless long been associated with a stable core of developers who have accompanied the company from its first platformers to today's major action titles, and with long-term leadership that has managed to carry the studio through several console generations without losing its creative identity.

## Today

Insomniac Games today operates as a fully internal Sony studio, focusing primarily on expanding the world of Marvel's Spider-Man and on further entries in the Ratchet & Clank series, which rank among the technological showcases of the PS5 console. The studio remains one of the most productive developers in PlayStation's portfolio and regularly delivers titles that define the platform's lineup for a given generation. Thanks to the combination of its own brands and major licensed projects, Insomniac, unlike many other studios, enjoys long-term security within Sony, and its games are often among the first titles meant to show what a new generation of PlayStation consoles is technically capable of.
io-interactive:
IO Interactive is a Danish studio that gave the gaming world one of the genre's most distinctive characters — a bald hitman with a barcode tattooed on the back of his head. The Hitman series is one of the few that has managed to consistently defend the concept of stealth action built on planning, disguises, and a creative approach to eliminating a target instead of straightforward shooting. Through it, IO Interactive earned a reputation as a studio that knows how to build sprawling, systemically rich levels where players discover dozens of ways to reach their goal on their own.

## History

The studio was founded in Denmark and built its identity almost entirely on the Hitman series, which it launched with the first installment, Hitman: Codename 47. This game introduced the series' core idea — the cold-blooded Agent 47, who must reach his target through sprawling, meticulously designed locations, whether through silent elimination, disguise, or engineering a seemingly unfortunate accident. The sequels Hitman 2: Silent Assassin and Hitman: Contracts gradually refined the series and expanded its repertoire of options, while Hitman: Blood Money is still considered one of the high points of the classic era thanks to its elaborate rating of the player's style and nonlinear mission design. In the meantime, IO Interactive also worked on other projects, including the action game Freedom Fighters, though none of them reached the same significance as the flagship series. After Hitman: Absolution, which partially moved away from the traditional stealth approach toward a more linear story, the studio returned to open-ended design with the series reboot simply titled Hitman, released episodically. This approach continued in Hitman 2 and Hitman 3, which together formed the so-called World of Assassination trilogy. Over the years, the studio also underwent changes in ownership structure, at one point becoming independent from its then-publisher and gaining greater control over its own brand and future direction. The episodic release model of the Hitman reboot, with individual locations rolled out gradually over the course of a year, was an unusual step for a major action series at the time. This approach, combined with an emphasis on mission replayability and the variety of paths to the same goal, became a hallmark of the series' modern era and set it apart from other action titles built on linear forward progression.

## Key figures

IO Interactive's modern direction is closely tied to CEO Hakan Abrak, who led the studio during the period when it broke away from its then-publisher and became an independent, employee-owned company. It was precisely this independence that allowed the studio to retain long-term control over the Hitman brand and decide its future direction on its own, without the direct influence of a major publishing house. Names from the studio's earliest history in the nineties, however, changed so much over the decades that it would be risky to track them down and list them without certainty.

## Today

Today, IO Interactive continues to develop the World of Assassination universe, a unified release that brings together the previous Hitman installments under one platform and is complemented by ongoing new content for modern consoles and PC. At the same time, the studio is trying to expand its portfolio beyond its best-known brand and is venturing into new projects outside the world of the hitman, though Hitman remains its main, most prominent, and commercially most important project. Thanks to its independence, IO Interactive can set its own pace for releasing new content and decide which direction its work will take next, making it one of the few major stealth studios to have retained authorial control over its most significant series.
larian-studios:
Larian Studios is a Belgian studio that worked its way up from relatively modest beginnings to the top of the computer RPG genre. For many years it was primarily a matter for devoted fans of isometric role-playing games, until Baldur's Gate 3 turned it into one of the most talked-about game studios of the present day. Its journey is a textbook example of patiently building a craft — from smaller projects through its own original series to taking over one of the genre's most legendary brands.

## History

Larian Studios built its reputation gradually on the Divinity series, which it opened with Divine Divinity, an isometric action RPG drawing inspiration from genre classics while adding its own distinctive humor and gameplay systems. The studio worked on the brand for years afterward, with each installment gradually expanding the world, the combat system, and multiplayer options. The turning point came with Divinity: Original Sin II, which combined a deep system of environmental interactions, cooperative play, and nonlinear storytelling into a form that earned acclaim from both players and critics, with the game later receiving an expanded Definitive Edition on additional platforms. This success opened the door for Larian to a much larger project — taking over the Baldur's Gate license, a legendary brand tied to the origins of the modern computer RPG. Baldur's Gate 3, built on the experience gathered during the development of Divinity, combined the rules of the Dungeons & Dragons tabletop game with a vast, reactive world and became one of the most successful and acclaimed RPGs of its generation. By releasing the game simultaneously on PC and the new generation of consoles, Larian confirmed that it could carry its ambitious projects through even beyond its traditional base. Throughout, the studio maintained its independence from major publishing houses, financing its growth mainly from the success of its own titles, which allowed it to gradually open additional offices in various European countries and expand its development team as the ambitions of individual projects grew. This gradual, seemingly unremarkable growth from a small Belgian studio into one of the most respected teams in the genre is now often cited as an example of how patience and focus on a single genre can, in the long run, bring greater success than chasing short-term trends.

## Key figures

Larian Studios has long been associated with its founder and creative director, Swen Vincke, whose vision and direct connection to the RPG genre shaped the studio's direction from its early titles all the way to Baldur's Gate 3. Vincke has long positioned himself publicly as the studio's main creative voice, the person behind decisions on game systems and overall tone, and is also the one who has long represented the studio externally in its presentations and communication with the player community. Details about other key figures within the wider development team, however, would not be appropriate to elaborate on without certainty.

## Today

Larian Studios today ranks among the most respected RPG studios in the world, and after the massive success of Baldur's Gate 3 it expanded with additional offices in various countries, giving it a significantly larger production capacity than it had during the development of the first Divinity. At the same time, the studio has repeatedly stated publicly that once support for Baldur's Gate 3 is finished, it wants to return to its own original projects outside licensed brands, continuing the history it built on the Divinity series. Thanks to the success of Baldur's Gate 3, Larian has earned a reputation as a studio that can combine the depth of a classic RPG with accessibility for a wider audience, and this position gives it considerable freedom in choosing which projects to pursue in the future.
level-5:
Level-5 is a Japanese development studio that, over two decades, worked its way up among the most distinctive creators of RPGs and family-friendly adventures. While big studios like Square Enix built mainly on established brands, Level-5 carved its own path with original worlds — from action RPGs with city-building elements through classic turn-based adventures to a puzzle series that became a phenomenon on handhelds worldwide. The studio is also notable for how often it collaborated with prominent figures from other fields, whether musicians, artists, or entire animation studios, giving its games a distinctive visual and musical signature that set them apart from the rest of Japanese RPG output. To this day it remains one of the companies capable of turning a single good idea into a long-running series spanning several console generations.

## History

Level-5 was founded in Japan in the late nineties and gained wider recognition among players in the early 2000s with Dark Cloud for the PS2 — an action RPG that combined dungeon crawling with the unusual element of building and rebuilding towns using collected items and materials. The sequel Dark Cloud 2 deepened this concept, expanded the combat system, and added a more elaborate story, showing that the studio was capable of experimenting with gameplay mechanics beyond the genre conventions of its time. A turning point came with the collaboration with Square Enix on Dragon Quest VIII, where Level-5 managed to meet the high expectations surrounding one of the most significant Japanese RPG series of all, later porting the game to the Nintendo 3DS handheld as Journey of the Cursed King. Equally important was Rogue Galaxy, a sci-fi action RPG that built on the experience of previous titles and offered a sprawling space story with a memorable cast of characters.

In the middle of the decade, the studio opened an entirely new chapter with the Professor Layton series, a puzzle adventure for the Nintendo DS that combined logic puzzles and riddles with a gripping detective story, becoming one of the most successful handheld concepts of its time, with numerous sequels and spin-offs. The same period also produced the tactical RPG Jeanne d'Arc for the PSP, drawing inspiration from the history of Joan of Arc. Another major step was the collaboration with Studio Ghibli on the Ni no Kuni series, which combined the visual style of the renowned animation studio with Level-5's elaborate RPG system — first on the PS3 with Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch, later on the PS4 with the sequel Ni no Kuni II: Revenant Kingdom, which moved away from turn-based combat toward a more action-oriented approach and expanded the series with strategic elements of managing one's own kingdom.

## Key figures

Behind the studio's founding and long-term direction stands Akihiro Hino, who serves as a key creative and executive figure across most of Level-5's flagship titles and has long set the direction the company follows as a whole. The studio is also known for regularly bringing in notable external collaborators from music, art, and literature for individual projects, thanks to which series like Ni no Kuni or Professor Layton gained a distinctive atmosphere that went beyond the usual standards of the game industry and attracted even players who otherwise take little interest in Japanese RPGs.

## Today

Level-5 remains an active Japanese developer and publisher that continues to develop its established brands while also seeking out new projects, and occasionally collaborates with other studios and publishers on ports and remasters of its classic titles for modern platforms. Series like Professor Layton and Ni no Kuni still retain a loyal audience even years later, and the studio continues to reference their legacy in its newer games.
lucasarts:
LucasArts was a game studio under George Lucas's empire that became synonymous in the nineties with top-tier graphic adventures. While other studios of that era built on action or simulation, LucasArts became famous for its emphasis on clever humor, elaborate dialogue, and inventive puzzles – its adventures remain among the most-cited examples of the genre to this day. The studio also benefited from access to the Star Wars brand, which it transformed into a range of action and flight games. The combination of its own original series and a powerful film license made LucasArts one of the most distinctive names in the gaming industry of the nineties, and its legacy is still visible in the work of many later studios that carried on the adventure genre. For many years, LucasArts thus represented an exceptional combination of the writers' creative freedom and the technical backing of a major media company – a feat rarely repeated in the game industry.

## History

The studio was founded as the game division of George Lucas's production company and benefited from the outset from its proximity to both the film industry and the company's technological resources. It played a key role in the development of so-called point-and-click adventures – in the first half of the nineties it released a string of titles that remain genre classics to this day: the Monkey Island sequels, Day of the Tentacle, Sam & Max Hit the Road, and Full Throttle. These games were known for their emphasis on storytelling, distinctive humor, and puzzles that couldn't be solved by randomly killing off the character as in rival adventures. At the same time, LucasArts developed the Star Wars license, producing not only adventures and action titles but also flight simulators and shooters – among them Star Wars: Dark Forces, one of the successful responses to the wave of Doom-inspired games. Toward the end of the nineties the studio released the adventure Grim Fandango, now considered one of the genre's high points thanks to its unconventional setting and visual style. Gradually, however, the market for classic adventures shrank, and LucasArts shifted its output increasingly toward Star Wars action games, such as the Republic Commando series. Alongside adventures and Star Wars titles, LucasArts also released a number of successful strategy and simulation games throughout the nineties, proving that the studio didn't rely on a single genre but could cover a broad portfolio of gaming experiences. In the following years, the LucasArts brand continued mainly as a publisher and producer of games from external studios, until the company, as part of the Lucasfilm empire's reorganization under Disney, ceased to operate as a development studio.

## Key figures

We deliberately do not name specific developers and leading figures, since we would have to rely on uncertain memory – but it remains a fact that LucasArts was known for its adventures being dominated by a strong authorial approach from individual creative teams, which gave games like Monkey Island and Grim Fandango a distinctive and recognizable signature. It is precisely this emphasis on the individual teams' distinctive writing and design signature that remains the main reason players and critics keep returning to LucasArts's classic adventures.

## Today

As an independent development studio, LucasArts no longer exists – after Lucasfilm's move under Disney, its development arm was wound down and the Star Wars brand moved to other publishers and studios. Nevertheless, LucasArts's legacy lives on in the form of remasters and remakes of its classic adventures, as well as in the inspiration that creators of narrative games still draw from its titles today. The LucasArts brand itself also remains the property of the Star Wars-centered corporation, so it occasionally still appears at least as a publisher logo on reissues of older titles, even though it no longer has a development team of its own like the one that made it famous in the nineties.
lucasfilm-games:
Lucasfilm Games was the in-house game studio of George Lucas's film company, which grew from a mere side experiment into one of the most respected adventure-game studios in history. While other publishers in the 1980s bet on action titles derived from film licenses, Lucasfilm Games went its own way, focusing on point-and-click adventures that emphasized humor, story, and playfulness. The studio's name is still associated with the Monkey Island, Maniac Mansion, and Indiana Jones series, and with the SCUMM technology that gave its adventures an unmistakable style and let players experiment without the game punishing them with the character's death. At a time when rival Sierra adventures routinely let players die over a single wrong step, this approach was far more player-friendly and helped the genre reach a wider audience.

## History

The studio was founded in the early 1980s as the game division of Lucasfilm, a company that was primarily a film production house. The first years were spent searching for its own identity – it produced action and arcade titles such as Rescue on Fractalus! and Ballblazer, which showcased the team's technical skill but not yet the direction that would make the studio famous. The turning point came in 1987 with the release of Maniac Mansion, an adventure built on the newly developed SCUMM system (Script Creation Utility for Maniac Mansion). This tool made it possible to create graphic adventures with intuitive control via commands, and later a mouse, without the need to type text commands as in rival games from Sierra or Infocom.

Maniac Mansion was followed by further successful adventures – Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Graphic Adventure, and in 1990 two key works at once: Loom and The Secret of Monkey Island. Monkey Island became the studio's flagship and launched a series that continued with further installments even after the studio was renamed LucasArts in the early 1990s. The studio gradually built a reputation as a maker of adventures with exceptionally well-written dialogue and a philosophy that players should never be able to unwinnably lose the game through an unlucky choice. Key to this shift was also the introduction of a simpler control interface with command verbs, and later a purely icon-based menu, which further lowered the barrier for new players and became a model for the entire adventure genre in the 1990s.

Besides adventures, the studio occasionally ventured into other genres, such as the action game Zombies Ate My Neighbors for the SNES or Star Wars: Yoda Stories for the Game Boy Color, showing that its creative range extended beyond the adventure genre. At the same time, the studio also worked on games tied directly to the Star Wars film brand and on flight simulations such as Their Finest Hour: The Battle of Britain, proof that Lucasfilm Games was not strictly a single-genre publisher, even though it built its name primarily on adventures.

## Key figures

The studio is inseparably linked with the name Ron Gilbert, who was behind the creation of the SCUMM engine and co-authored Maniac Mansion and The Secret of Monkey Island. Alongside him, writers and designers Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman contributed to key titles and later founded their own successful studios. This generation of creators defined the humorous, self-deprecating tone that set Lucasfilm Games's adventures apart from more serious rival games.

## Today

The Lucasfilm Games brand was renamed LucasArts in 1990, under which the studio continued producing adventures and action games tied to the Star Wars brand until the early 21st century. LucasArts itself was closed in 2013 following Disney's acquisition of Lucasfilm, but the Lucasfilm Games name was revived several years later as a label for game projects developed under the Lucasfilm banner in collaboration with external developers. The original studio's legacy lives on independently of the official name as well – classic adventures like Monkey Island and Maniac Mansion have received remastered releases and remain a favorite target for retro gamers even decades after their original release.
microprose:
MicroProse ranks among the most significant American game studios of the 1980s and 1990s and is inseparably linked with the simulation genre – whether aircraft, submarines, or tanks. The company was known for its meticulous emphasis on realism and technical authenticity in its simulations, which earned it respect from both players and military and aviation enthusiasts, who appreciated its attempts to replicate the actual handling and behavior of real equipment as faithfully as possible. At the same time, MicroProse is home to the strategy series Sid Meier's Civilization, one of the most influential strategy games of all time, which still defines the entire genre of turn-based civilization-building strategy games. The studio thus stood at the crossroads of two seemingly different worlds – precise military simulators and thoughtfully designed turn-based strategy – and achieved extraordinary influence on the further development of both genres and on generations of later game creators.

## History

MicroProse was founded in the early 1980s by Sid Meier and Bill Stealey, with Stealey bringing military experience and business leadership while Meier was the main creative force behind the game designs. The company quickly established itself as a specialist in flight and military simulators for home computers, such as Solo Flight and F-15 Strike Eagle, and gradually expanded its portfolio to include submarine simulations, such as Silent Service, and ground combat vehicles. These titles were released on the popular platforms of the time, including the Commodore 64 and DOS, and combined technical authenticity with gameplay accessible to a wider audience.

A major turning point came with the release of Sid Meier's Railroad Tycoon at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s, which showed that the studio could also successfully build economic and strategic simulations outside a military framework. This line culminated in 1991 with Sid Meier's Civilization, which defined the entire genre of turn-based civilization-building strategy games and became one of the most influential games in the history of computer gaming. MicroProse continued to develop its flight simulators with the F-15/F-19/F-117A series and military titles such as Gunship 2000, maintaining two parallel strong brands – one built on the technical authenticity of military simulators and the other on thoughtful strategic gameplay.

In the 1990s the studio also embarked on further strategic and tactical projects, among them the turn-based X-COM series, to which it contributed as publisher, and continued developing Civilization with a second installment. At the same time, however, the company went through a period of frequent organizational changes typical of the game industry at the time, when smaller studios merged into larger publishing groups. During this period MicroProse underwent several changes of ownership and mergers, and its fate and brand gradually dissolved into larger publishing entities, while its key creators and their most successful series, above all Civilization, continued under new companies.

## Key figures

Sid Meier is the most significant creative figure associated with MicroProse – he took part in designing a number of flight simulators as well as the creation of Railroad Tycoon and Civilization, which defined his reputation as one of the most influential game designers in history. Bill Stealey co-founded the company and handled its business and organizational operations, especially in the early years when the studio established itself as a specialist in military simulators.

## Today

The original MicroProse no longer exists as an independent company in its former form – during the 1990s and 2000s it was gradually absorbed into larger publishing structures, and its brand disappeared for a time. The studio's legacy nevertheless lives on, above all through the Civilization series, now developed by Firaxis Games, a company founded by former MicroProse creators, and in recent years the MicroProse name has also reappeared in the form of a newly revived brand associated with publishing simulators.
naughty-dog:
Naughty Dog is one of the most acclaimed development studios in console gaming history, closely tied to the PlayStation brand, for which it has long developed exclusive titles. It has made its name with several generation-defining series, from the mascot platformer Crash Bandicoot through the action-adventure Jak and Daxter to the prestigious action series Uncharted and The Last of Us, which rank among the most acclaimed and commercially successful games on Sony's platforms. The studio is known for its emphasis on cinematic storytelling, technical sophistication, and continually pushing the boundaries of what the current generation of consoles can achieve graphically and narratively.

## History

Naughty Dog was founded before the rise of the PlayStation console and in its early years worked on smaller projects, before fully focusing on collaboration with Sony in the mid-1990s. The first major step toward that partnership was the fighting game Way of the Warrior for the 3DO console, after which the studio moved on to developing for the original PlayStation. A defining milestone came with the platformer Crash Bandicoot, which made Naughty Dog one of the key studios of the first PlayStation generation and turned its title character into an unofficial mascot of the console for a time. The series continued with further installments and the racing spin-off Crash Team Racing.

After the transition to PlayStation 2, the studio replaced Crash with the new series Jak and Daxter, which combined platforming elements with a more open world and, with further entries Jak II and Jak 3, gradually shifted toward a more action-oriented, darker tone, including the racing spin-off Jak X: Combat Racing. This transition demonstrated the studio's ability to leave behind a successful brand and build a new one from scratch, a pattern Naughty Dog would repeat several more times in the years that followed.

The real turning point came with the PlayStation 3 generation, when the studio launched the Uncharted series, an action-adventure inspired by adventure and action films that, thanks to its cinematic storytelling and technical polish, earned great acclaim from players and critics alike starting with the very first installment, Uncharted: Drake's Fortune. The series continued with Uncharted 2: Among Thieves and Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception, which further refined the cinematic pacing and technical execution of the games. Building on Uncharted, Naughty Dog then followed with the even more ambitious project The Last of Us, a post-apocalyptic story about the relationship between its two main characters, still considered one of the high points of storytelling in the gaming medium. The studio went on to further develop both series on PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5, including Uncharted 4: A Thief's End and Uncharted: The Lost Legacy, as well as remastered and expanded editions of older titles.

## Key figures

Naughty Dog was founded by Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin, who led the studio through its early years and the Crash Bandicoot and Jak and Daxter era. After their departure, Neil Druckmann and Bruce Straley became the key creative figures, directing and writing the Uncharted and The Last of Us series and significantly shaping the studio's emphasis on cinematic storytelling and emotionally resonant characters.

## Today

Naughty Dog is today part of Sony Interactive Entertainment and remains one of the flagship development studios of the PlayStation platform. The studio focuses on further developing and maintaining its key brands, above all The Last of Us series, which it is gradually expanding into other media, and continues to hold a reputation as a team that defines the technical and narrative standard for exclusive PlayStation games. Older series such as Crash Bandicoot and Jak and Daxter are no longer developed by Naughty Dog itself, but their legacy lives on through remasters and sequels entrusted to other studios, while Naughty Dog itself remains focused on large, technically and narratively ambitious projects.
nihon-falcom:
Nihon Falcom is among the very oldest Japanese development studios and still holds a reputation as a maker of honest RPGs with an emphasis on story, music, and long-term continuity of the game world. While major studios like Square or Enix expanded over the years into dozens of genres and formats, Falcom has stayed true to action and tactical RPGs, and from this narrow specialization has drawn two massive series — Ys and The Legend of Heroes — which have become synonymous with old-school Japanese RPGs. The company is a prime example of a studio that never needed to be the biggest player on the market to build a loyal and remarkably patient audience, spanning from PC-98 home computers in the 1980s to today's consoles and PC. In a genre where many studios experiment with format and presentation, Falcom instead has long deepened just a handful of game worlds — and that is precisely where its unique standing lies.

## History

Falcom was founded at the turn of the 1970s and 1980s as one of the first Japanese computer game developers and quickly established itself on the PC-98 platform, the standard of Japanese home computers at the time, on which the vast majority of domestic game production outside of consoles was then being made. It was there, in 1987, that Ys I: Ancient Ys Vanished was released, an action RPG that, thanks to its fast combat system, clear visuals, and unforgettable synthesizer soundtrack, kicked off one of the longest-running game series ever. A year later came the sequel Ys II: Ancient Ys Vanished – The Final Chapter, which concluded the story and cemented the studio's position as a specialist in action RPGs emphasizing pace, clarity, and atmosphere over complex systems.

The same era saw the launch of the second key series — Dragon Slayer: The Legend of Heroes in 1990, which over the following decades spun off into the standalone Trails branch, today one of the most extensive and elaborately crafted RPG sagas on the market, renowned for its interconnected world and politically charged plots. Falcom also experimented outside these two main brands, for example with the action-adventure Brandish in 1991 or the charming Popful Mail, which was first released on PC-98 and three years later got a reworked version for the Sega Mega-CD.

The transition from PC-98 to modern consoles happened gradually — Falcom long remained a strongly Japan-focused phenomenon whose games reached the West only sporadically and with considerable delay. It was not until the 2010s that its titles began to be systematically localized and released on PlayStation Vita, PS4, Switch, and PC in the same year as, or shortly after, their Japanese release. Titles such as Ys: Memories of Celceta, Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of Dana, or the Trails of Cold Steel series finally brought the studio to an international audience, without it abandoning the distinctive genre signature and craftsmanship fans had grown used to since the PC-98 era.

## Today

Nihon Falcom still operates today as an independent studio focused almost exclusively on continuing Ys and Trails, both series releasing at regular, nearly annual intervals on current consoles and PC, and regularly receiving remasters of older installments for new platforms. The company maintains a reputation as a reliable, if fairly conservative, publisher — it doesn't bet on major technological leaps or fashionable trends, but on continuity of its story universe, well-crafted characters, and loyalty to its longtime fans. Those fans appreciate that its creators aren't afraid to stick to their own, long-proven path even amid major shifts in the games industry, at a time when many other studios change direction with every new trend. More than four decades into its existence, Falcom thus retains its position as a small but remarkably stable player in the field of Japanese RPGs, whose games keep receiving regular remasters and new installments regardless of how the rest of the market shifts around it.
nintendo-epd:
Nintendo EPD, in full Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development, is Nintendo's largest internal development wing and the creator of the vast majority of brands we associate with the company at first thought today — Zelda, Mario, Splatoon, Animal Crossing, or Ring Fit Adventure. It was formed by merging two historic divisions and has since been behind the overwhelming majority of the Switch console's flagship titles. For players, EPD is synonymous with Nintendo's precision — games that appear playful and accessible at first glance but hide remarkably refined game design beneath the surface, something the company has taken great care over for decades.

## History

Nintendo EPD was formed in 2015 by merging two long-standing divisions — Nintendo EAD (Entertainment Analysis & Development), which had been behind the Mario and Zelda series since the days of the NES and SNES, and Nintendo SPD (Software Planning & Development), focused more on smaller projects and collaboration with external studios. The goal of the merger was to unify internal development capacity under a single leadership and allocate teams across projects more efficiently.

The new division fully demonstrated its strength with the arrival of the Nintendo Switch in 2017 — delivering several major titles in the very first year alone: the open world The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, the platformer Super Mario Odyssey, the racer Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, and the shooter Splatoon 2. This wave defined the early period of the Switch and showed that EPD could work on many major brands in parallel. In the following years came further successes — the creative tool Super Mario Maker 2, the fitness title Ring Fit Adventure, which became a phenomenon, and Animal Crossing: New Horizons, which accompanied millions of players through the pandemic period in 2020.

EPD continued releasing new entries in established series — Splatoon 3, Nintendo Switch Sports, the long-awaited Zelda sequel Tears of the Kingdom, and Super Mario Bros. Wonder, which returned to 2D platforming. With the arrival of the Switch 2 console in 2025, the division again delivered both launch and follow-up titles, among them Mario Kart World and Donkey Kong Bananza, confirming its role as the main engine of Nintendo's first-party output for the new hardware generation as well.

## Key figures

Overseeing the entire division and its projects for the long term is **Shigeru Miyamoto**, the legendary designer behind the creation of the Mario and Zelda series, who holds one of the highest creative oversight roles at the company. The Zelda series has long been shaped by producer **Eiji Aonuma**, who has been responsible for the direction of the brand since the days of Ocarina of Time. Director **Hidemaro Fujibayashi** played a key role in the creation of the open world of Breath of the Wild and its sequel. Among the leading figures is also **Yoshiaki Koizumi**, who has taken part in producing a number of major projects, including Super Mario Odyssey.

## Today

Nintendo EPD remains, in 2026, the main internal development pillar of Nintendo and is behind the vast majority of major exclusives for the Switch and the emerging Switch 2. The division continues to develop dozens of brands in parallel — from action-adventures through racing games to sports and fitness titles — and its games regularly rank among the best-selling and best-reviewed on the market. Given the division's size and the scope to which it covers Nintendo's portfolio, EPD remains one of the most important development centers in the entire games industry.
obsidian-entertainment:
Obsidian Entertainment is an American studio that has built a reputation as a specialist in deep RPGs with an emphasis on story, moral ambiguity, and freedom of choice. It grew out of people who worked on classics like Fallout and Baldur's Gate, carrying that experience into its own projects. The studio is known for taking someone else's franchise and giving it a depth few would expect elsewhere – Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II and Fallout: New Vegas remain among the most cited examples of a sequel surpassing the original in writing and systems. For RPG fans, Obsidian is synonymous with writing full of gray areas and decisions with no clearly right answer.

## History

The studio was founded in 2003 by veterans of Black Isle Studios, Interplay's in-house RPG team, who had helped establish the isometric computer RPG genre with games like Fallout and Icewind Dale. They immediately put that experience to use on their first major project, the sequel Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II, which despite a troubled development and unfinished content earned a reputation as one of the best-written games in the Star Wars franchise. Neverwinter Nights 2, another computer adaptation of the Dungeons & Dragons rules, followed.

A turning point came with Fallout: New Vegas in 2010, which the studio made on contract for Bethesda using the previous game's engine and on a fairly tight development schedule. The game expanded the post-apocalyptic American setting with factional politics and a reputation system, and to this day many players consider it the high point of the entire series. After years of working on other companies' franchises, the studio struck out on its own – in 2015 it released Pillars of Eternity, a return to isometric RPGs inspired by classics like Baldur's Gate, largely funded through crowdfunding on Kickstarter. Its success showed that demand for traditional computer RPGs hadn't disappeared, only that major publishers had stopped meeting it. The sequel, Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire, expanded the world with a pirate theme and seafaring, and deepened the faction and reputation system the studio had already built on in Fallout: New Vegas.

In 2019 the studio released The Outer Worlds, a sci-fi RPG with a strong streak of black humor and criticism of corporate profit-chasing, still as an independently published project. Shortly before that, in 2018, Microsoft acquired Obsidian and folded it into Xbox Game Studios, giving the studio a more stable footing for future development. Smaller, more experimental projects followed – the survival game Grounded and the narrative Pentiment, set in historical Bavaria and praised above all for its inventive writing and manuscript-inspired visual style. In 2025 the fantasy RPG Avowed was released, set in the same world as Pillars of Eternity.

## Key People

The studio was co-founded by Feargus Urquhart, who had previously led Black Isle Studios and helped create the classic computer RPG genre, and who still heads Obsidian today as its CEO. Alongside him, other developers with roots in the teams behind Fallout and Baldur's Gate helped found the studio, bringing from Black Isle Studios experience in writing branching dialogue and reputation systems – and this emphasis on choices and their consequences still shapes most of Obsidian's projects today, regardless of whether it's their own IP or work-for-hire for another publisher.

## Today

Since 2018, Obsidian Entertainment has been part of Microsoft under Xbox Game Studios and continues developing RPGs both in its original worlds, such as Pillars of Eternity and Avowed, and in smaller narrative projects. Even under a major publisher, the studio has kept its reputation as the genre's maker of games with the strongest emphasis on storytelling.
origin-systems:
Origin Systems was one of the most important American game studios of the 1980s and 90s, famous above all for the Ultima series, one of the founding pillars of the computer RPG genre. The studio earned a reputation for ambitious, technically demanding games with elaborate worlds and a moral system that, in Ultima, determined how the world around the player reacted to their actions. Besides RPGs, Origin also became known for the space action series Wing Commander, which served as a technology showcase for what PCs of the era could do. The company motto "We create worlds" captured the studio's ambition to build vast, believable game universes – even at the cost of high development expenses, which later became one of the reasons for its demise.

## History

Origin Systems was formed in the early 1980s around the creator of Ultima, who had begun developing the series even before the company was formally founded. The small publisher gradually grew into a studio with its own development team, and thanks to the success of subsequent Ultima installments it built a strong position in the DOS computer game market. A pivotal step was the launch of the Wing Commander series in the early 90s, which combined action-packed space combat with cinematic storytelling and hired actors in video sequences – at the time one of the most expensive productions on PC.

In the early 90s the company was bought by publisher Electronic Arts, which allowed the studio to finance ever more ambitious projects, including the technically demanding Ultima VII and Ultima VIII as well as further generations of Wing Commander. Origin was among the pioneers of multimedia storytelling in games, with Wing Commander featuring extensive live-action film sequences, and it experimented with unconventional platforms too, such as releasing Wing Commander III for the VFX1 headset or the 3DO console. Alongside its flagship series, side projects emerged as well, such as the Jane's line of flight simulators, which expanded the studio's portfolio with more realistic military themes.

A defining moment came with the release of Ultima Online in 1997, one of the first mass-successful MMORPGs, which showed that the genre's future lay in persistent online worlds shared by thousands of players at once. Despite this success, however, rising development costs on individual projects and several commercially weaker titles led Electronic Arts to gradually scale the studio back. The last major single-player entry, Ultima IX: Ascension, came out in 1999 to mixed reviews, and a few years later Electronic Arts closed the studio, focusing instead on keeping Ultima Online running under other teams.

## Key People

The studio's central figure was Richard Garriott, known by the nickname Lord British, who created the Ultima series and shaped its characteristic emphasis on moral choices and an elaborate game world. Around him, Origin Systems built a creative team capable of developing two demanding franchises in parallel – the RPG series Ultima and the action series Wing Commander – and later responsible for the move to online play in the form of Ultima Online.

## Today

Origin Systems ceased to exist as an independent studio in the early 21st century after Electronic Arts gradually absorbed it and eventually shut it down. The Ultima and Ultima Online brands, however, survived under various teams within EA, and the Origin name still appears today, for instance, on the publisher's digital distribution platform, even though it no longer has anything to do with the original development studio. Origin Systems' legacy lives on above all among fans of classic RPGs and in communities dedicated to preserving and keeping older Ultima titles running today, whether through fan-run Ultima Online servers or by keeping alive the memory of the influence the early Ultima and Wing Commander games had on the entire computer game genre.
platinumgames:
PlatinumGames is a Japanese studio renowned for action games built on precise combat systems, exacting timing, and a bold visual style. It grew out of teams that defined the character action genre in Japan, and it remains one of the few studios able to build a game purely around how well it plays – without an open world, crafting, or the endless grind that characterizes most big action titles today. Titles like Bayonetta and Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance became synonymous with stylish, fast, technically demanding combat and influenced an entire generation of action games. For fans of the genre, PlatinumGames is a mark of quality, even though the commercial success of individual games has often failed to match their artistic ambitions.

## History

PlatinumGames was founded in 2006 in Osaka, in part by former Capcom developers who had previously been behind the shuttered Clover Studio – creator of games like Okami and Viewtiful Joe. That experience with a bold visual style and inventive game design became the foundation of the new studio's identity. Its first major release under the new name was MadWorld for Wii – a stylized black-and-white bloodbath that showed the studio could bring brutal action even to a console aimed at a broader audience. The real breakthrough, though, was Bayonetta in 2010, which quickly ranked among the generation's best action games and launched a long-running series. The same year saw the release of Vanquish, a sci-fi shooter emphasizing speed and tactical sliding, which, despite modest commercial success, earned a cult reputation.

The studio further defined itself through collaborations with major publishers on other companies' franchises – Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance was made in partnership with Konami and showed the team could stamp its style even on someone else's license. Similarly, The Wonderful 101 for Wii U combined action with an original idea of controlling heroes by drawing shapes. Its relationship with Nintendo produced the sequels Bayonetta 2 and 3, exclusive to Wii U and Switch, while a collaboration with Square Enix on Nier: Automata in 2017 gave the studio one of its greatest critical and commercial successes, thanks in part to a striking story and music that went beyond the usual action game. Later, the studio also tried its hand at its own intellectual property, such as the action game Astral Chain for Switch, which linked the player character's combat to controlling a supernatural companion on the other half of the screen.

## Key People

The studio is closely tied to the name Hideki Kamiya, one of its co-founders, who helped establish the character action genre back in the days of Capcom and Clover Studio and, at PlatinumGames, was behind the creation of several key titles, including Bayonetta. Alongside him, other experienced creators from the Japanese action scene, who had followed a similar path through Capcom and Clover Studio, contributed to the studio's distinctive visual and gameplay signature, which allowed PlatinumGames to keep a recognizable style across the various franchises and publishers it has worked with over the years.

## Today

PlatinumGames continues developing action games today while also working long-term to establish its own intellectual property independent of contract work for major publishers, which in the past has helped the studio survive periods when several internal projects failed to make it to release. It remains one of the few specialists in the character action genre, and even after all these years its name is, for players, a guarantee of quality and a fluid combat system – though the road to long-term financial stability hasn't always been easy, and the studio has had to lay off staff and cancel projects in the past. Even so, it remains a name that action game fans associate with a high craft standard and the courage to try unconventional game mechanics.
remedy-entertainment:
Remedy Entertainment is a Finnish development studio that has built a reputation for atmospheric action games with a distinctive cinematic signature. It rose to fame with the Max Payne series, its dark noir story and bullet time effect becoming one of the most imitated gameplay mechanics of the turn of the millennium and inspiring numerous other action titles that tried to replicate that same sense of slowed-down time. Since then, Remedy has stayed true to its style — games full of psychological tension, unconventional storytelling, and strong visual design, where gameplay blends with film and television elements, whether through cinematic cuts, live-action footage, or an episodic story structure. The studio is among the smaller ones that has nonetheless managed to build a loyal fanbase and a reputation as an auteur creator in an environment dominated by major publishing brands, thanks in part to its willingness to experiment with storytelling forms in ways much larger studios often don't dare attempt.

## History

Remedy Entertainment was founded in Finland in the 1990s, and even before its worldwide breakthrough it was behind the isometric action game Death Rally, which mixed racing with devastating vehicle-mounted weapons. The studio achieved truly widespread recognition with Max Payne, released in collaboration with Rockstar Games. The game combined a noir story with an innovative slow-motion mechanic during shootouts and became both a commercial and critical success that defined the third-person genre for years to come. The sequel, Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne, deepened the storyline and confirmed that the studio could combine action with emotional storytelling.

After parting ways with the Max Payne brand, whose rights remained with Rockstar Games, Remedy struck out on its own and began building original worlds that gave it full creative freedom. Alan Wake for Xbox 360 delivered a psychological horror inspired by television, divided into episodes reminiscent of a TV series, in which the main character, a writer, grapples with darkness seeping into his own story. The game didn't take off commercially right away, but over the years, thanks to its atmosphere and unusual storytelling, it built up cult status and spawned the spin-off Alan Wake's American Nightmare as well as a much later direct sequel.

The studio went on to experiment with storytelling combined with live-action footage in Quantum Break, where gameplay chapters alternated with episodes performed by real actors. The turning point then came with Control, which introduced the distinctive world of the Federal Bureau of Control and cemented Remedy's reputation as a studio capable of creating its own strong brand without relying on older IP. Remedy gradually began linking its games into a unified fictional world it calls the Remedy Connected Universe — Control contains references to Alan Wake and hints that the two worlds intertwine. Alan Wake 2, after years of waiting, then fully developed this connection and confirmed that Remedy holds on to its identity even in the era of new consoles. In the meantime, the studio also took on a smaller detour outside its own brands, collaborating on CrossFire X, a shooter derived from the Asian online hit CrossFire.

## Present

Today, Remedy Entertainment continues developing its own connected universe around Control and Alan Wake and is working on further projects building on the success of recent years, including a cooperative spin-off set in the world of Control. The studio is gradually making its older titles accessible to new generations of players as well, as shown by the remastered release of Alan Wake Remastered for current consoles and PC. The studio has maintained its position as a respected creator with a distinctive authorial signature that remains recognizable across console generations and shifting publishing partnerships.
rockstar-north:
Rockstar North is a Scottish development studio based in Edinburgh that is the main creator of the Grand Theft Auto series. The studio carries on the legacy of the earlier DMA Design team and is responsible for the entries that defined the entire open-world action genre — from Vice City through San Andreas to Grand Theft Auto V, one of the commercially most successful entertainment productions in history. Rockstar North belongs to publisher Rockstar Games and parent group Take-Two Interactive, and its games are known for expansive open worlds, a satirical view of American society, and technical ambition that has repeatedly pushed the boundaries of what current consoles and computers could handle.

## History

The studio's roots trace back to the Dundee-based company DMA Design, which became famous in the eighties and nineties for the platformer Lemmings and later for the first Grand Theft Auto, which introduced a top-down view of criminal mayhem in an open city and gave players unprecedented freedom to choose between obeying the law and breaking it. After being acquired by publisher Take-Two and folded into the newly formed Rockstar Games label at the end of the nineties, the studio was renamed Rockstar North and shifted its creative focus to the GTA series, which it also transformed into a fully three-dimensional form.

The breakthrough moment was Grand Theft Auto III, one of the first titles to bring the open-world concept into three-dimensional space with a free-moving camera, immediately followed by Vice City, set in a fictional version of 1980s Miami, and San Andreas, with a sprawling state inspired by California and Nevada. These entries catapulted the series among the best-selling brands in the games industry and also showcased the studio's signature style — sprawling maps inspired by real American regions, an elaborate soundtrack featuring licensed music from period radio stations, and dark humor aimed at pop culture and American society.

With the arrival of Grand Theft Auto IV, set in the fictional Liberty City inspired by New York, the studio focused on a more realistic take on story, characters, and vehicle physics. The following Grand Theft Auto V then took the open-world concept to a previously unseen scale thanks to three playable protagonists and the city of Los Santos, inspired by Los Angeles and its surroundings. The game was released gradually across several console generations as well as on PC and became one of the commercially most successful entertainment titles ever, partly thanks to the online multiplayer mode GTA Online, which the studio, together with other Rockstar Games teams, has long expanded with new content, activities, and vehicles.

## Key figures

The studio carries on the legacy of David Jones, co-founder of DMA Design and a key figure behind the creation of both the first Grand Theft Auto and the earlier hit Lemmings, even though he was no longer involved in later work under the Rockstar North name and left the company shortly after the studio's renaming. The longtime face of Rockstar North itself was Leslie Benzies, who led the studio for many years and took part in the production leadership of the development of key entries in the series from Grand Theft Auto III through Grand Theft Auto V, before the paths of Benzies and Rockstar Games parted after years of collaboration.

## Present

Rockstar North remains the main development studio of the Grand Theft Auto series within Rockstar Games and continues to focus on expanding Grand Theft Auto V and its online component, while also working on further entries in the series for the coming generation of players. Even after more than two decades, the studio maintains its position at the technological forefront among developers of open game worlds.
ryu-ga-gotoku-studio:
Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio is a Japanese development studio under Sega, responsible for the Yakuza series — known in Japan under its original name, Ryu ga Gotoku. The studio has built a reputation for games that combine gritty crime drama set in fictional districts inspired by Tokyo and Osaka with a completely unrestrained side content offering full of minigames, karaoke, baseball, darts, and absurd humor. Thanks to this combination of a serious story and boisterous side entertainment, the series has become one of the most distinctive Japanese brands of the modern era, and the studio has gradually expanded its scope beyond the action-adventure genre — including the detective spin-off series Judgment and a shift to turn-based combat inspired by classic Japanese RPGs. For many players outside Japan, Yakuza serves as an entry point into modern Japanese game design, as it combines local atmosphere with storytelling accessible to Western audiences as well.

## History

The studio has its roots in an internal Sega team that, from the mid-2000s, worked on developing the first Yakuza for PlayStation 2. The game introduced the main character Kazuma Kiryu and the fictional district of Kamurocho, inspired by Tokyo's Kabukicho, and combined the style of B-movie yakuza films with a sophisticated combat system and extensive side content. The success of the first entries led the development team to formally become independent as Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio, allowing it to focus fully on the long-term development of the brand across console generations.

A turning point for the series' international perception was Yakuza 0, a prequel set in the 1980s, which new players often cited as the ideal entry point thanks to its accessible storytelling and more aggressive marketing outside Japan. It was followed by a wave of remasters of older entries for PlayStation 4, allowing players to catch up on the extensive saga surrounding Kiryu before the series reached his story's conclusion in Yakuza 6: The Song of Life.

At the same time, the studio also experimented outside the main line. It created the detective spin-off Judgment, set in the same game world but with a different protagonist and an emphasis on investigation mechanics and tailing characters through the streets of Kamurocho. The truly decisive turn, however, came with Yakuza: Like a Dragon, which introduced a new protagonist, Ichiban Kasuga, and reworked the combat system from action-based to turn-based, drawing inspiration from classic Japanese RPGs. This move divided part of the loyal fanbase but opened the series to an entirely new audience and gave it the new subtitle Like a Dragon, under which it is also released internationally. Subsequent entries such as Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth further developed this direction, while smaller titles like Like a Dragon Gaiden or the remake Ishin! served as bridges between individual chapters of the story and made older content accessible to a new generation of players.

## Key figures

For most of its history, the Yakuza series was embodied by producer and director Toshihiro Nagoshi, who was present at the birth of the first entry while still at Sega and set the tone for the whole brand for many years — both its serious criminal storyline and its bizarre side content. Nagoshi left Sega after many years to found his own studio, while leadership of Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio passed to a new team, which guided the series through its shift to turn-based combat and to the new protagonist Ichiban Kasuga.

## Present

Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio today continues as an active part of Sega, still alternating major mainline entries with smaller spin-off projects and remasters that bring older titles to current platforms. The Like a Dragon brand has become one of the pillars of Sega's current lineup, and the studio regularly ports its games to new console generations as well, as shown by the release of Yakuza 0 Director's Cut on Switch 2. At the same time, the studio continues developing both branches of the series in parallel — Kazuma Kiryu's action-based legacy and the new turn-based style built around Ichiban Kasuga.
snk:
SNK is a Japanese studio and hardware company whose name has been inseparably linked, since the nineties, with arcade fighting games and the Neo Geo system. While Capcom ruled home consoles and the gaming mainstream, SNK built a reputation as a maker of games for the most demanding audience — arcade-goers who wanted fast, technical, and visually over-the-top duels. Series like Fatal Fury, Samurai Shodown, King of Fighters, and Metal Slug made it one of the few companies able to compete with Capcom long-term in the fighting game space, and at the same time a symbol of luxurious, expensive gaming hardware of its era. The Neo Geo, priced close to a small car, became a legend precisely because it offered an arcade experience at home, with no compromises on graphics or gameplay.

## History
